title: Why a Test Can't Tell You Your 'Biological Age'
description: There's no simple number that can reveal the full truth about your health.
fullText:
It's not enough to live forever—everybody wants to stay young forever, too. In most wellness spaces, "youth" is a word that gets thrown around as synonymous with "health," but you don't have to be into woo-woo wellness culture to find yourself tempted to find out how old—or more accurately, how young—you really are. Maybe you can't fight your chronological age, but you can find comfort in an alternative framing: "biological age."

The pitch is appealing. Send in a vial of blood or a tube of spit, pay several hundred dollars, and receive a number that supposedly reveals your "true" biological age. The promise is that this age is the one your body is actually living, as opposed to the one on your driver's license. If you find out you're "biologically" 35 instead of 45, the implication is that you've pulled one over on the passage of time. Discover the reverse, and the tests often come bundled with supplements, programs, or subscriptions designed to fix your problems.

The real problem is that biological age isn't actually a single figure that can be measured or calculated, and no test—however promising the science behind it—can hand you a definitive verdict on how your body is aging. Here's what's actually going on inside these tests, what legitimate research says about aging, and how to think about the growing market of products promising to quantify your youth.

Chronological age is easy: you count the years since you were born. Biological age is an attempt to pin down how well your body is actually functioning relative to that timeline. Dr. Dan Belsky, an epidemiologist at Columbia University who studies aging, explains it this way: Everyone moves through calendar time at the same rate, but "the conditions inside our body obviously vary." Because health tends to decline over time, biological age is essentially an estimate of the age at which a person's physiological integrity—how well their organs and tissues function, resist stress, and recover from injury—would be considered typical within some reference group.

That last part is key. "There really is no ground truth biological age, because it's always relative to some expectation," Belsky says. Saying you're "biologically 25" only means something once you know what factors you're being judged on, and what standards you're being compared to. A biological age score is a construct built from a specific reference population, which could be a large, nationally representative sample, or a much smaller research cohort. That detail is key to understanding how much weight any individual result should carry.

Consumer biological age tests love to reduce aging to a single number, but researchers who study aging combine many types of data to get anywhere close to a meaningful picture. That typically includes laboratory-based biomarkers, like the kind of bloodwork your doctor might order during an annual physical. Those biomarkers are then placed alongside clinical measurements like blood pressure, heart rate, and imaging. Increasingly, researchers also look at molecular and cellular markers, including genes and proteins.

One of the most talked-about approaches in recent years uses "epigenetic clocks," which look at chemical modifications to your DNA (rather than the DNA sequence itself) and compare the pattern to population averages to estimate biological age. Several companies now sell consumer versions of this technology, generally priced around $300, using blood or saliva samples.

According to Belsky, at their best, these commercial tests are "a consumer implementation of a research tool." In practice, that means a lab takes an algorithm developed using a specific research dataset and applies it to your individual sample. The algorithm was built to describe patterns across groups, not to diagnose an individual person, which is part of why a single test result can deliver an unreliable personal verdict.

When it comes to what actually shapes biological aging, the answer is "almost everything," Belsky says. Genetics play a role in how resilient a person's body is over time. But environmental and behavioral factors are often just as important, if not more so. The quality of the water you drink and the air you breathe, your diet, and the stability and meaningfulness of your social relationships are critical. Sleep, exercise, and nutrition tend to dominate the public conversation, and for good reason, but they're part of a much longer list of contributing factors.

This is also where biological age intersects with inequality. Research has consistently linked poverty, pollution, and unstable living conditions to accelerated biological aging and shorter lifespans. Not everyone has equal access to fresh food, clean air, safe housing, or reliable medical care—and those disparities show up in the body over time. A biological age test can't account for the structural conditions someone is navigating; it can only reflect the downstream biological signal.

This is where the marketing gets ahead of the science. Many products claim you can measurably "reverse" your biological age through supplements, specific diets, or intensive protocols. The research, naturally, is more cautious. From the standpoint of how most people intuitively understand biological age (as a general reflection of your body's current state), yes, that state can be modified through better health habits. But whether behavioral, environmental, or pharmacological interventions actually change the pace of aging at the cellular level in humans? There we have "less clarity," Belsky says.

Of course, living a healthier life will generally support how your body functions, and likely influence the biomarkers that feed into these tests. But claims that a particular product has been shown to "reverse" cellular aging in a rigorous, replicated way should always be treated with skepticism. Despite the promises of certain longevity influencers, there's no evidence that any supplement, cold plunge protocol, or red light therapy device will add decades to your life.

It's also worth reframing the goal. Healthy aging isn't really about looking younger than your birth certificate suggests, or avoiding every illness. Instead, it could be more productive to think in terms of a broader health span: the stretch of life you spend active, capable, and free of major disability. That means building habits that help your body adapt as it inevitably changes with time, rather than wasting your time, money, privacy, and mental health in the pursuit of a lower number on a test result.

If you are itching to find out your "true" age, consider treating your score as a simple data point, as opposed to a catch-all verdict. "People often want a yardstick to track progress toward personal wellness goals," Belsky says, "and the best-evidenced tests have at least been studied in research settings, so there's some understanding of how their scores relate to disease risk, disability, mortality, and in some cases, how responsive they are to interventions." At the same time, "these are not standalone, one-shot measurements you can trust to reveal the full truth about your health." Like any biomedical test, they're subject to bias and error, and they need to be interpreted alongside other health information, ideally with a healthcare professional.

Before spending a few hundred dollars on a biological age test, it's worth asking yourself a more practical question: Let's say you find out your body is aging "faster" than your birthday suggests—how would you actually change your behavior? Perhaps a biological age test is the helpful nudge you need to jump-start habits you've been meaning to build anyway. But if you already generally know the factors that support long-term health—moving your body, eating well, sleeping enough, managing stress, maintaining relationships, avoiding smoking, and so on and so forth—maybe you can start making those changes today, no vial of blood required.

title: Big tech says AI can find a cure for cancer. So where is it?
description:
Alongside warnings about its ability to destroy humanity, artificial intelligence is also hailed for its potential to revolutionise health treatment. Just how far can it take us?
Her name was June. June would be the last month she ever knew.
I remember the way her bed made her so small, swallowed her up in the middle of the room, turned as it was to face the window.
fullText:
Her name was June. June would be the last month she ever knew.

I remember the way her bed made her so small, swallowed her up in the middle of the room, turned as it was to face the window. With her liver failing, her skin was a ghostly apricot. June – I called her Nan – had been stalked by the king of terrors, the emperor of all maladies: cancer. That son of a bitch.

The cancer was in her pancreas. Odds of survival? “Not good” – putting it lightly. The maths, putting it darkly: it’s the 12th most common cancer worldwide, the sixth most common cause of cancer death. The World Health Organization says it is “one of the cancer types with the least favourable prognosis”. It was not favourable for my grandmother.

June died nine years ago. Lately I’ve been thinking about alternate futures – the ones in which my grandmother, and the many millions diagnosed with cancer each year, are still here. The thoughts creep in as we are bombarded by artificial intelligence chief executives making bold proclamations such as “AI will cure cancer in five to 10 years” or “AI will cure cancer in our lifetimes”. Those claims stand in contrast to apocalyptic scenarios, including AI being responsible for human extinction before 2030. AI, we hear, is both saviour and annihilator.

Park the world-ending scenarios and you’ll find there has been significant progress in using AI as a tool in the detection, prevention and treatment of cancer. If there is a future where a supposed AI apocalypse is averted, then it may be one in which cancer therapy has been completely redefined. But just how far can AI take us towards a cure?

Today AI is being turned toward drug development, treatment plans and, in some places, it’s being used clinically, studying imagery of lungs for early signs of malignancy and helping to remove brain tumours. Words like “efficiency” and “personalised care” are everywhere; the notion AI can free up time for doctors and medical professionals to get away from the busywork abound.

Even with such positive advances, speak to clinicians, oncologists and researchers working at the coalface and you quickly find there is tension between the more grandiose claims of big tech and its race to “solve” disease, and the deliberate, considered progress of science.

“Until AI can actually think and do experiments itself at scale, I’m not sure that we’re going to find a cure for all cancer or medical illness in the next 10 years,” says Sherene Loi, a medical oncologist who specialises in breast cancer treatment at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Melbourne.

But Loi and other cancer experts the Guardian has spoken to believe there will be efficiencies for treatment, diagnostics and pathology services that will bear fruit, heralding more personalised and more equitable cancer care.

Cancer is not a single disease. It’s a catch-all term that describes the uncontrollable growth of abnormal cells. Typically, we describe cancers based on the location within the body that they are found: breast, prostate, lung, brain, blood, pancreas. These are complex, highly variable diseases, affecting a variety of different cells and underpinned by a host of genetic changes. In addition, cancer outcomes depend on many factors, including the biology of the disease and the treatments available. A single cure for cancer is not only unlikely but nigh on impossible.

Just take the brain. Though not all are cancerous, “there are more than 100 types of tumours in the brain, much more than in any other single organ”, says Felix Sahm, a neuropathologist at the University Hospital Heidelberg. “There are so many unresolved questions in brain tumour research and brain tumour care.”

We’ve made great leaps in cancer survival rates over the past century; chemotherapy and radiation have enabled solid tumours to be cured, monoclonal antibodies ushered in more direct targeting of abnormal cells, and emerging treatments are rewriting how we combat the disease. But, as Loi notes, “Human disease is very complex.” So where does AI fit in?

“AI can improve several parts of that process by helping us identify risk, detect disease, characterise tumours, select treatments and monitor,” says Ajit Goenka, a radiologist and nuclear medicine specialist at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota.

Medical imaging, in particular, stands to benefit from advances in AI and machine-learning models. Training models on huge amounts of patient data, such as CT scans, X-rays or tissue samples, enables those models to detect changes or patterns that may be imperceptible to the human eye.

Goenka has been exploring the early detection of pancreatic cancer with machine-learning tools since 2021, before the release of ChatGPT fully turned the public’s head toward generative AI. Since then, OpenAI and its rival Anthropic have pushed into new realms beyond chatbots: partnering with companies to accelerate access to treatment; striking deals with research centres; and working with pharmaceutical companies to incorporate large language models and AI into drug discovery.

Goenka noticed that some patients who developed pancreatic cancer had undergone CT scans months or years before diagnosis. Those scans were interpreted as normal but Goenka reasoned there could be microscopic, measurable changes invisible to a radiologist. “We began studying whether quantitative imaging and machine-learning methods could detect that signal,” he says.

In a proof-of-concept paper published in 2022, he confirmed that hunch. Machine-learning tools can detect pancreatic tumours, including in pancreases that appeared normal, before clinical diagnosis. Further studies by Goenka’s group have explored how robust and reproducible the method is and whether it is useful across institutions. The opportunity, he says, is to identify evidence of cancer earlier. My grandmother’s pancreatic cancer appeared as if out of nowhere, a shadow on a scan. Goenka’s models may have been able to see it sooner, which could have improved her outcome.

Sahm leads a European multi-disciplinary collaboration called EUcanAI, which is using agentic AI to improve the way brain tumours and central nervous system cancers are treated. The idea is that “every single chunk of this journey gets informed by the previous one and informs the next one in the sequence, so that it gets more efficient, quicker and less cumbersome for a patient”, he says.

He provides one example of a teenager who presented with a tumour in his brain stem. The expectation was that it was fatal, based on imaging and the patient’s age. The patient went in for surgery, his tumour was biopsied and rapidly sequenced to determine the mutations driving his disease.

Traditionally, these results go to a board of specialists to discuss the next steps in surgery and treatment. But today, these results can be delivered during a surgery, saving patients time and money. Sahm imagines a world where agentic AI accelerates this process even further – a surgeon could biopsy and image a tumour, then have an AI provide answers about the kind of mutation and potential drugs that may treat it. Sahm says this work is already happening in trials but stresses it is not yet routine.

The key for Sahm is a more tailored journey for each patient that “reduces the duration of uncertainty”. It’s about providing a wholly optimised approach to managing a patient’s cancer journey. He also notes it could provide more patients with better care.

This was a common thread in discussing AI tools for cancer diagnostics. “I think it will help with regards to equity of care, and access to care,” Loi says.

For instance, she says, in rural communities or locations that do not have cancer facilities or access to specialists or specialist diagnostic tools, access to machine-learning models could help medical professionals provide faster, more complete answers.

The dream of curing cancer is one that big AI firms constantly seed. Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, has suggested that within a decade, cancer – and many other diseases – could be cured. The Google DeepMind spin-off, IsoLabs, has a bold mission statement to “solve” all disease.

Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, has similar lofty goals, suggesting the ability to solve disease might just be a problem of how much computing power backs our AI systems. “Maybe with 10 gigawatts of compute, AI can figure out how to cure cancer,” he wrote. As AI firms experience growing backlash to the environmental cost of datacentres, the argument that just a little more compute could offer life-saving opportunities could be hard to sell.

But Emilia Javorsky, a physician and scientist at the Future of Life Institute, argues the opposite: “We cannot compute the fundamental truth of biology, we can only measure it.”

In her March essay on AI and cancer, she outlines the complicated process of developing and testing any new medication. “Thirteen years into the AI drug discovery movement, we still lack a single [Federal Drug Authority]-approved drug that cleared the full bar of regulatory approval, reimbursement, and clinical adoption,” she says.

Javorsky argues that curing cancer is a noble goal but the research community must be smart about where investment goes. It’s not intelligence that limits progress but the data, regulation and incentives that surround cancer research.

Even if all the data from research across the world was placed into these models, would that be enough to solve these diseases today? What about in five or 10 years? For Sahm, there are biological truths we are yet to uncover. In his work, he still encounters rare, unknown pathology that doesn’t “fit into a box”. While AI may be able to devise technology or tools to understand rare subtypes, it’s only as good as its training data.

The complexity of human physiology and biological processes comes up a lot in discussions with those working in cancer. Although AI may speed up the process of, for instance, hypothesising and creating new drugs that can treat specific forms of cancer, it is fundamentally limited in applying those learnings to the real world. “Someone actually has to go back and do the experiment, right?” Loi says.

An article published in The Australian newspaper in March revealed that a Sydney data scientist had been able to synthesise a bespoke cancer vaccine for his dog, Rosie, by uploading her genetic information to ChatGPT. And while some were astounded by the development, others noted that the hard work had still been done by humans in a lab.

Even if AI can determine the most effective targets for new drugs, it cannot cut through red tape. Sahm notes that the majority of AI-assisted or AI-led research being performed is experimental and remains in clinical trials. Even if AI tools were deemed safe for test patients, he says, the EU lacks a clear regulatory path to allow them to reach the market. “That ends up in a lot of AI research going on, a lot of surprising and promising things happening … but also surprisingly few of those really being applied,” he says.

The most vocal proponents of AI – those building the models – may make grand claims about cures but on the ground the reality is different. There’s a lack of understanding of cancer complexity, many researchers working in the space argue.

But it’s clear that AI does provide a sense of hope for clinicians and researchers. Alone it cannot dethrone the king of terrors; it cannot bring down the emperor of all maladies. Curing cancer will require more than extra-efficient computation.

“AI can come up with a million hypotheses,” Loi says – but we will still need humans to help understand which of them are true.

“Technology,” says Goenka, “is only one part of the answer.”

fullText:
People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisis

A December 1969 report from the consumer magazine Which? explored a relatively new gadget that, it predicted, many people would be giving as Christmas presents: the electric toothbrush. For those who hadn’t yet seen one, the magazine described it as “not that much different in principle from an ordinary brush – you have a stick with a brush on the end. The difference is that an electric one moves the brush head for you”. Progress indeed.

Nearly six decades on, electric toothbrushes can do a lot more than merely jiggle, offering multiple speeds and movement sensors for real-time tracking of where you’ve brushed – some even promise gum-massage or tongue-cleaning modes. Prices range from about £25 for a basic Oral B model to £599.99 for a Philips Sonicare model that gives “smart coverage feedback”. The latest super-toothbrush – a mere £419.99 – features a camera and a built-in water jet to clean between teeth, using AI to identify gaps. Created by Dyson, it’s still, essentially, a stick with a brush on the end (although there is another toothbrush on the market that’s shaped like a mouthguard, with individual brushes, that claims to clean your teeth in 20 seconds).

In the UK, 59% of adults use an electric toothbrush and sales, including replacement heads, reached £361m in the last year, according to market intelligence company Mintel. Any product launch by Dyson – still associated with reinventing the vacuum cleaner – feels like something of an event, so its incursion into oral health does feel significant, says Rachel Bairsto, the head of museum services at the British Dental Association. “We’re seeing more and more expensive toothbrushes,” she says. “Expensive toothpaste as well.”

These highly designed everyday objects have become symbols of affluence. “If you see a picture of a swanky bathroom, it will definitely have plug sockets for some kind of rechargeable electric toothbrush,” says Bairsto. “Whereas I’ve tried to look through the archives to find pictures of bathrooms with toothbrushes in them, and I can’t. Was everybody appalled at the sight of a toothbrush in the bathroom? I don’t know.” With many toothbrushes now, she says, “I think there’s definitely a status symbol [aspect] to it.”

We’re more interested in oral health than ever, says Dr Zaeem Jafri, a dentist and the founder of Nova Smiles, an online advice website. “From what I’ve seen from my patients, people are more conscious about it, wanting to avoid dental treatment, wanting their teeth to look nice and feel nice, and I think a lot of people are turning to gadgets to help.” Another dentist, Dr Reena Wadia, known as Dr Reena, a periodontist or gum specialist at the RW Perio clinic in London, says: “Gum health has become super topical. One reason why is because there’s really good evidence now that gum health is linked to your general health, so gum health is now part of the wellness conversation. People are taking it more seriously.” There is growing evidence that gum disease, she says, comes with an “increased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Those are the two key ones, [but] there’s lots of other conditions related to it.” A poor oral microbiome has been associated with a range of diseases, including Alzheimer’s and several types of cancer, as well as depression.

Both Dr Reena and Jafri recommend rechargeable electric toothbrushes over manual ones, but neither are urging their patients to go out and buy a Dyson brush, or spend similar sums on other brands. “There’s no robust research that says a certain kind of electric brush removes plaque at a better rate than others,” says Jafri.

Jafri has tested Dyson’s CameraJet, along with many other electric toothbrushes. He found it messy – the water jet was hard to angle, and he says it didn’t seem to find all the gaps between his teeth. He points out that a non-foaming toothpaste is needed for an adequate camera view – sold by Dyson, with the cheapest at £8.49. The live stream to a phone app was a novelty, but in reality he says it was hard to see much with water, teeth and the inside of his cheeks in the way. Cameras in toothbrushes, says Jafri, “have the potential to be good. If patients had cameras that were detecting chipped and broken fillings and can send those images to a dentist to review [and] spot things early, that would be a phenomenal advancement. For Dyson right now, it’s using the camera to detect when the brush is in the right position to shoot the water jet – it didn’t really work that well for me. It’s a bit of an overkill.”

Another concern is that the water jet rinses away the toothpaste when most dentists now recommend spitting, not rinsing, so the fluoride in it stays on and around the teeth for longer. Dr Reena adds: “[The water jet may] make people think, oh, I don’t need to floss, or I don’t need to use interdental brushes. But actually, that jet is an adjunct, not a replacement.” Niamh Turney, a Dyson engineer who worked on the CameraJet, says, however, “The goal is to make interdental cleaning easier and more convenient for those who aren’t already managing to fit flossing into their routine.”

There have been reports of some brushes overheating, and charging problems; at the time of writing, the brush was unavailable to buy. Dyson says it is aware that “a small number of early batches may have experienced a component issue. We are isolating those batches and are taking all the necessary steps to support our customers,” and that there are “some shortages of supply as we are in the process of scaling up production. We expect the next wave to be available in the coming weeks.”

Meanwhile, we are in the midst of an oral health crisis. It is slowly improving on previous years, but access to NHS dentists remains low – 60% of the adult population in England have not seen an NHS dentist in the two years to March 2026. Inequality has a huge effect on oral health – in the most deprived areas, adults are less likely to brush their teeth twice a day, and children are more than three times more likely to have tooth extractions related to decay. The proportion of adults who use an electric toothbrush is 47% in the lowest income groups, compared with 76% in the highest income. Jafri says that the people who are considering spending hundreds of pounds on an electric toothbrush, or those who track their brushing on apps, are likely to be “health-conscious individuals who are brushing their teeth well to begin with, and [this is] probably not solving the bigger problem we have”.

The first electric toothbrushes, says Bairsto, had a “clunky side-to-side action, and that’s about all they could do.” There was an increased interest in dental and oral health in the 1960s – programmes to add fluoride to drinking water were rolled out – and electric toothbrushes were part of this, even if they were slow to take off. That 1969 Which? report tested “all 11 we could find on the market”, including those made by Bosch and Boots, alongside several by US manufacturer Ronson, more famous at the time for its cigarette lighters. Women, it claimed, preferred brushes with a softer touch; men liked something more vigorous “as you might expect”. Children liked them, the report said, “perhaps because they are a good way of doing action paintings with toothpaste on the bathroom mirror”.

Now the market is dominated by Oral B, owned by Procter & Gamble. Jafri says dentists don’t earn commission from selling products but, he adds, “in dental school, they come in with free pizzas and give everyone an Oral B brush. All the dental students kind of associate with Oral B quite quickly. There will be the ‘Oral B lecture’ that everybody talks about because it’s free pizza.”

It has a market share of approximately 60% according to Ziyu Tian, a personal care research analyst at Mintel. “Other brands like Philips, [own labels such as] Superdrug and Boots, and Colgate are also the big players,” she says. The Dyson launch, says Tian, while a premium product that won’t appeal to everyone, will raise the bar for consumer expectations and may force existing players in the sector to innovate. Alongside the increased awareness around oral health’s links to general health, she says, “teeth whitening and the beauty element of oral care is something that the younger generation is really embracing. So oral care is not only about cleaning the teeth or freshening the breath, it’s more about the beauty and wellness routines in general.”

As more evidence emerges, particularly links to the gut microbiome, companies will lean on this in their marketing, says Tian. You can already see it in products such as toothpaste that contains “prebiotics and probiotics for our microbiome, magnesium for evening wind-down, and exosomes [“messengers” between cells, already used in skincare] for tissue regeneration, anti-ageing and longevity”. Toothpaste flavours are branching out, too, from the traditional mint, with berries, chocolate and even fried chicken. “I think it is tied to the rise of the GLP-1 [weight loss injections],” says Tian. “Consumers might not get these indulgent flavours from food and drink, and oral care like toothpaste and other things can be a substitute.”

One of the more recent incomers to the toothbrush market is Suri (from £65), launched in 2022, which makes nicely designed, recyclable, largely plastic-free electric toothbrushes. Its founders, Mark Rushmore and Gyve Safavi, both previously worked in marketing for Procter & Gamble. They were driven, says Rushmore, by the environmental impact of toothbrushes. “Billions of brushes are thrown away – manual, electric – and end up in landfills and oceans. Every brush you’ve probably ever used since you were a child still exists somewhere.”

Damien Walmsley, an emeritus professor of dentistry at the University of Birmingham, has worked with all the big powered toothbrush companies, and most recently with Suri. He says he is probably still under non-disclosure agreements so won’t go into detail; “but I’ve seen some wacky ideas out there, some strange ones”. Companies are constantly trying to add new features, “so that people feel they’re getting a newer product, and people will then be attracted to it. If it’s something new, it will catch the imagination, and that’s what this new Dyson has done.” If it encourages people to brush their teeth more effectively, and more often, “that’s really good”. But Walmsley questions how long the novelty lasts. “We’d like to see more long-term studies evaluating the cost. Was it worth paying the extra money, and did it bring about extra value from that? Those studies aren’t out there.”

Walmsley was one of a number of scientists involved in the 2003 review of literature by the Cochrane library, with the latest update in 2014, concluding that powered toothbrushes were more effective in removing plaque than manual brushes – by 11% in the short term, and 21% after three months – and at reducing gingivitis (early-stage gum disease). Many of the studies were small, short-lived – and run by Oral B. Should consumers be concerned about that? Research studies are expensive, says Walmsley, and over the years Oral B was among the few companies doing them. “We have certain criteria, and we checked that [studies] followed that, and we followed up the evidence,” says Walmsley. “It was as open as it can be.” He also points out that toothbrushing technique and usage in a controlled trial may be different compared to use by a wider population in everyday life.

“Dental professionals should be showing their patients how to brush,” says Dr Reena. “It sounds basic, but actually, [many people have] never been shown. Essentially brushing along the gum line [at around a 45-degree angle] to remove bacteria that are trapped. The bristles should be going under your gum line a little bit.” But not too hard, which can lead to gum recession. A pressure sensor is a valuable feature. “Different modes [in speed for instance] are quite helpful as well, if someone’s got sensitivity or gum issues.” She is interested in the idea of a camera in a toothbrush, especially if it can provide “real-time feedback on what a patient is doing. But the key thing it always comes back to is that technique and consistency are more important.”

The Houston Texans claimed Johnson off waivers before releasing him and paving the way for his return to Baltimore for his second stint. fullText:
WASHINGTON – Senate Republicans' three-month headache about Mitch McConnell's health seems to have subsided – at least for now.

In the days since the Kentucky lawmaker's return to the Capitol, they've defended him in the halls and expressed gratitude that his condition has improved. A fall in June, followed by a bout of pneumonia, kept the 84-year-old off the job for much of the summer and complicated the voting math for Senate Republicans on key legislation.

On his way back into the Senate chamber on the night of Monday, Sept. 14, he joked with reporters about admittedly dodging their questions since he'd been gone. Sitting in a wheelchair with visibly bruised hands, he resolved that it was "time to get back to work" and "finish the ​job for this Congress." He isn't running for reelection and will end his more than 40-year Senate tenure by January.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, who's served in the Senate with McConnell for more than a decade and will also retire next year, said he had a "great conversation" with him on Thursday. It was "classic Mitch," Tillis told USA TODAY.

"I spent 20 seconds asking him how he's doing, and he goes right into preserving the filibuster, and who we have to look ahead to do it as we leave, and Ukraine," Tillis said.

McConnell has been a vocal proponent of maintaining U.S. military and diplomatic support for Ukraine amid its ongoing war with Russia, as well as shielding the filibuster, the 60-vote threshold in the Senate that he says encourages bipartisanship, from President Donald Trump's campaign to eliminate it.

His reemergence in the Capitol took the internet by storm. One moment in particular stood out: During a meeting of the Senate Agriculture Committee to vote on the farm bill, it appeared to some onlookers as though McConnell voted incorrectly, raising more questions about his mental state.

When McConnell voted yes, Sen. John Hoeven, R-North Dakota, leaned over and said something to him. But Hoeven told USA TODAY he wasn't correcting McConnell – he himself wasn't sure about whether they were taking a more procedural vote or voting on final passage of the bill out of committee.

"He voted, and he voted correctly," Hoeven said. "He was there. He was present. He got it right."

Hoeven and other Senate Republicans said they were happy to have McConnell back. The Senate will be in session for another two weeks before going on recess for more than a month until after the midterm elections in November.

"I haven't had a chance to run into him," Rand Paul, McConnell's Kentucky counterpart in the Senate, told USA TODAY. "But I'm glad he's back and glad he's doing better."

Zachary Schermele is the congressional correspondent for USA TODAY. Reach him by email at zschermele@usatoday.com and on Signal @zachschermele.02. Follow him on X at @ZachSchermele.

title: Do the Apple Watch Series 12's New Health Features Live Up to the Hype?
description: I have the newest Apple Watch in my hands, and I've already begun putting its newest features to the test.
fullText:
I now have the Apple Watch Series 12 in my hands—or, rather, on my wrist—and have spent the past 24 hours putting it through as many tests as I can manage. I'm pleased with the step counting and the availability of "recovery HRV" (as opposed to the cardiac-health-focused HRV that the Apple Watch previously used) but I'm not sure if the heart rate accuracy is living up to the hype. I'll be putting this device to more rigorous tests, but here are my first thoughts.

Apple waited forever to add step counting as an easily viewable metric on the watch, but it’s finally here. I can open my smart stack (with a double pinch of my fingers, not even touching the watch screen) and see my steps right on top. I’ve also added a step count complication to my watch face. You can find this complication under Activity. The option to see your rings as a complication is still there, but you can now also add steps or wheelchair pushes.

Step counts work well. They update quickly, and seem to be accurate in my casual counting—nine steps from my desk to the door registers as nine steps. I’ll do more in-depth testing soon, to properly evaluate Apple’s claim that it now has the most accurate step counting out there.

What’s disappointing is that it took so long—and that step counting is not coming to the Series 11 or any earlier watch. Apple’s step counting uses a special pedometer model that’s built into its new processor. Older Apple watches don’t have the hardware to calculate your steps as precisely, leading Apple to leave the feature off those watches. That is wild to me, considering that every other wearable has had step counts on the watch ever since the first cave dweller strapped a rock to their wrist.

Apple claims the Series 12 has the most accurate heart rate in a wearable, and I’ve already mentioned that that's a bold claim given what I’ve seen in the past from Apple and from other devices. Now that I have a Series 12 in my hands, I was able to do some preliminary testing.

To be totally clear, these are not thorough tests, and I’m not making a decisive conclusion based on just a few days’ testing. But I’ll show you what I’ve tried so far.

As always, I’m testing the device against my heart rate as read by a chest strap (the gold standard for heart rate comparisons). I did:

A treadmill interval run with the Series 11 and a chest strap

An identical treadmill interval run with the Series 12, a chest strap, and the Garmin Forerunner 570 for good measure

An outdoor run that included steady jogging, intervals, and walking, with the Series 12, a chest strap, and the 570.

I’m including the 570 in these tests because it has what I would consider the most accurate heart rate sensor in a wearable. In my past testing it’s reported numbers that were identical or nearly identical to the chest strap. That said, there’s always variation from day to day, and it didn’t shine quite as well in these recent tests compared to some I’ve done in the past.

Here are the indoor runs with the Series 11 on top, and the Series 12 on the bottom, both in red and both compared to a chest strap. The Series 11 was already doing a pretty good job, and to be honest I’m not sure if the Series 12 is any better. I’m disappointed that the Series 12 is still only sampling heart rate every five seconds during workouts. Other devices, like the chest strap and the Garmin, sample every second. That means Apple is taking 12 data points every minute while these other devices are taking 60.

Here’s the outdoor run. The chest strap is in gray, Garmin in blue, and Apple in red. Again, the sparse data points of the Apple watch aren’t impressive. I see a few places where Apple missed the peak of a small spike, but then again the Garmin struggled in a few spots as well. I’ll do further testing and report back when I’ve been able to try out the watch in a greater variety of activities and conditions.

Live Rewind and Siri Recaps aren’t available yet. Live Rewind is the feature where you can ask for a text transcription of whatever was said around you in the last 15 seconds. Recaps handle a longer timeframe—for example, to summarize a meeting. These features are coming later this year, and aren’t in the version of watchOS 27 that came with the watch. (I have not installed any beta software on the watch.)

Readiness is another big feature coming soon, but I haven’t logged enough nights of sleep to get my scores yet—it needs about a week of data. As a preview, I am seeing my “recovery HRV” listed with my sleep data. Last night my HRV was 45 according to Apple, and 50 according to my Oura ring. HRV readings from different devices may vary, depending on exactly when they take their measurements, so I’ll be looking for trends rather than specific data points. If both devices agree on what is a high or a low reading for me, given my baseline, I’ll call that a success for Apple.

fullText:
Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes

Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackle AI-generated fake imagery.

A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up by Facebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food.

The board said Meta’s safeguards were “consistently and fundamentally inadequate” to address the rapid rise of AI deepfakes.

“From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse,” said Pamela San Martin, an oversight board co-chair.

“These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation. Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes.”

In the Scotland clip, the councillor is falsely represented as saying: “Refugees are welcome here, even if they rape our women, because white people do that too.”

The oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, said the video of the councillor appeared to be AI-generated, as indicated by the audio not being fully synchronised to the unnamed councillor’s facial movements.

Even when raised directly with the company by the board, Meta decided the video did not violate its content policies and did not merit an AI label.

In a blogpost published on Thursday, the board said the post should have been removed because it violated Meta’s rules on hateful conduct by alleging criminal and predatory sexual behaviour by refugees as an entire group and not as individuals. The video should also have received a “high risk AI” label, said the board, as it called for tougher measures on deepfakes.

“The majority [of the board] finds that Meta needs more robust policies on deepfakes, including expanding the situations when ‘high risk’ labels can be applied, more measures to reduce the spread of deceptive AI content, increasing the penalties for accounts that repeatedly share it, and more transparency on data around when AI labels are applied,” it said.

The board recommended nine policy changes at Meta, including ensuring algorithms demote content labelled “high risk”, making such posts less likely to appear in users’ feeds. It also recommended that Meta makes it more difficult for users to view AI-generated content by, for instance, introducing a warning screen that requires a click-through before viewing the content.

In a separate ruling, the board also ordered Meta to take down from Facebook an AI-generated video mocking a young Muslim woman in Europe taking part in a campaign to improve menstrual health education and reduce stigma around health conditions for women and girls from ethnic minority backgrounds. AI-manipulated videos and images mocking the woman had tens of millions of views online, including on Meta platforms.

The board singled out one of the videos – showing the woman exercising absurdly and eating junk food – as a breach of the company’s bullying and harassment policy. It recommended the post be removed and made three policy recommendations, including changing its definition of “unwanted manipulated imagery” to cover deepfakes of a private individual saying or doing things they did not say or do.

The board was set up by Meta in 2020 to serve as a referee for content on its platforms. Meta has been approached for comment.

title: What an influencer turned surgeon general could mean for public health in the U.S.
description:
President Donald Trump's nominee for surgeon general, Dr. Nicole Saphier, faced her Senate confirmation hearing on Wednesday. - Jose Luis Magana/AP
Wednesday’s Senate confirmation hearing wasn’t the first time much of the American public met Dr. Nicole Saphier and heard her perspective; President Donald Trump’s nominee for US surgeon general is a health and wellness influencer who has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers through her podcast and social media platforms.
In some ways, the surgeon general position – often referred to as the nation’s doctor – is the original health influencer, tasked with translating science into terms that are easy to understand and guiding the public on ways to improve their health.
fullText:
Wednesday’s Senate confirmation hearing wasn’t the first time much of the American public met Dr. Nicole Saphier and heard her perspective; President Donald Trump’s nominee for US surgeon general is a health and wellness influencer who has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers through her podcast and social media platforms.

In some ways, the surgeon general position – often referred to as the nation’s doctor – is the original health influencer, tasked with translating science into terms that are easy to understand and guiding the public on ways to improve their health.

“For a decade, I have specialized in translating complex, fast-evolving medical information on various media platforms into content that millions of Americans can understand and use, including during the uncertainty of the global pandemic,” Saphier, a radiologist and Fox News contributor, said in Wednesday’s hearing.

“I realized then how badly this country needs public health communication that is straightforward and grounded in the best evidence available,” she said. “My years of communicating directly with the public have prepared me to explain complex topics in a way that they can understand.”

But experts say that social media has changed how people receive health information, with increasingly blurred lines as to who is considered to have authority and expertise – and that bringing an influencer into the role of surgeon general presents both opportunities and challenges.

Dr. Jerome Adams, who served as surgeon general during Trump’s first term, says the distinction between the role of an influencer and the role of the surgeon general matters more than the overlap.

“An influencer builds a brand and an audience. The surgeon general speaks for the nation (and not just ‘followers’), leads the Public Health Service Commissioned Corps, and has a duty to follow evidence even when it is politically inconvenient,” Adams said in an email to CNN. “Influence is a tool, but it is not the job.”

The Pew Research Center said in a report published this year that a significant share of the American public – 4 in 10 adults overall and half of those under 50 – now get their health and wellness information from social media influencers and podcasts.

But the center’s analysis of thousands of influencer profiles found a wide range of backgrounds, with less than half describing themselves as some kind of health professional. About 1 in 8 cite their personal experience in their social media bios, and nearly 1 in 6 do not mention anything about their background or expertise.

“Now, when a healthcare provider sees a patient, any number of other individuals and platforms and messengers have that patient’s ears and eyes,” said Eileen Yam, director of science and society research at Pew. “The ballgame is changing so quickly as far as where people hear health information, wellness information, beyond that kind of mainstream white coat expertise.”

Influencers presenting information from a clinical perspective may take a very different approach from those who base their content around personal experience, experts say, and there may be friction between the two approaches on the same topic.

“On the internet, there’s a lot of anecdotal information that gets generalized, but not everything is generalizable,” said Amanda Yarnell, senior director of the Center for Health Communication at Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

“I think some of the most successful creators, both in audience and in providing good information and making people connect with it, are people who have blended their personal experience with other expertise,” said Yarnell, whose center launched a program in 2023 that works directly with creators to use their social media platforms to counter health misinformation online and to spread evidence-based science.

Surgeon general nominee Saphier presents herself as someone who can balance that line between personal and professional experience. To her nearly 360,000 followers on X, she identifies herself as a “full time wife, mom and doctor.”

Her Instagram profile, where she has 147,000 followers, includes the same line – but also indicates that she is the “creator of Drop Rx,” a brand of liquid herbal supplements.

Her bio page on the Drop Rx site says she wanted to create “clean, thoughtfully crafted tinctures that support focus, calm, balance, and overall wellness” that are inspired by “traditional herbal wisdom and modern scientific insight.” The site notes that “statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration. Our products are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.” Many of the products are currently unavailable online. Some sell for $24.99 for 2 fluid ounces.

Business interests like this are part of what has challenged influencer credibility, experts say, especially as more traditional information sources like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have also lost some of the public’s trust around evidence-based recommendations.

“There is often financial gain involved with (social media influencing), so that can influence the content that is delivered as well,” said Dr. Anne Cappola, ​a ​physician and executive director of the Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. “It’s not always transparent to those who are absorbing that information. It’s all getting muddy.”

Generally, Pew found that only about 10% of US adults say they trust all or most of the information they get from influencers, while a quarter said they trust not much or none at all.

“The lion’s share of these audiences say that they trust some of the information. So there’s some healthy skepticism that people are using when they’re seeing information from health and wellness influencers overall,” said Galen Stocking, an associate director of research at Pew and lead author of the recent report.

As the public parses all of the health and wellness information that is available to them online, experts say that trust in the messenger becomes one of most important aspects of who they decide to listen to.

“Authority, benevolence and integrity are three pillars of how people have long thought about trust models,” Yarnell said. “The way (these pillars) show up on the internet is quite specific, and they can be used for good or bad.”

Former Surgeon General Adams said the trust Saphier has gained as a health influencer could ​serve her well as surgeon general, but maintaining that trust in a government role under the current administration will present new challenges.

He said he isn’t concerned about Saphier’s ability to communicate, but he is concerned about whether “the environment she would enter will let her tell the truth about what’s actually harming Americans, and how best to protect them” – particularly around vaccine-preventable diseases.

Saphier will have to work harder to establish credibility with those who are skeptical about her “prior association with a network and movement that many see as increasingly against science and vaccines,” he said. But she has an opportunity to reach groups “who have tuned out traditional public health voices” and to “raise trust among people who currently distrust ‘the establishment.’”

She’ll need a “clear, independent voice,” he said.

When asked about her views on vaccines in Wednesday’s hearing, Saphier said that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is “our greatest tool for combating measles,” and she said she does not believe that childhood vaccines cause autism.

But when Sen. Bill Cassidy directly asked her “Should a parent be vaccinating their child with the MMR?” she didn’t reply with a yes or no.

“I think that the recommendation is to combat what we are seeing right now – the best tool we have to combat these infections, to save the most lives and to also create population herd immunity – is vaccination against the MMR,” Saphier replied.

In a podcast episode in February, Saphier reflected on the role of surgeon general after a prior nominee – author, Stanford medical graduate and wellness influencer Casey Means – faced her Senate confirmation hearing.

“The biggest skill that this person needs is they need to be able to effectively communicate with the public, public health messaging,” Saphier said on her podcast.

“But even more important than that, they need the respect of not only the people, the American people that they are communicating to, but they also need the respect of the administration for which they are working together with to get that research and put out the messaging, and also the medical professionals, the medical organizations, they need to make sure that she is a trusted messenger.”

Trump withdrew Means’ nomination in April after the vote stalled in the Senate, replacing her with Saphier. (Trump had previously withdrawn the nomination of another surgeon general candidate, Dr. Janette Nesheiwat, a New York family physician and former Fox News medical contributor.)

Within days of her nomination, Saphier deleted numerous social media posts in which she broke publicly with Trump and US Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on some of the administration’s most politically sensitive health issues, including vaccines and autism.

Saphier changed her X profile to private soon after.

“A preexisting following is useful only if she uses it to defend science, not to soften it,” Adams said. “Trust in this role has never come from celebrity. It comes from consistency with evidence, and a willingness to speak out on behalf of health, even when it may be unpopular.”

fullText:
The University of Brighton says it is considering closing one of its three campuses from 2030 in favour of condensing its operation into two sites.

A spokesperson for the university says it hopes to move its operation from its Falmer campus to its City and Moulsecoomb sites, which it says will make it stronger and more sustainable.

No decision has yet been made to close the Falmer campus and it plans to consult on the changes, the university says.

Citing pressures on universities across the UK, it said: "We're choosing to shape our own future, building a university that is stronger, more sustainable and better connected to the needs of future students, employers, communities and partners."

Closing the Falmer campus would be supported by investment into its two other campuses, the university said.

Changes to the university could affect the university's library, currently based on the Falmer campus. About 600 students currently live in two halls of residence on the campus.

The campus also houses the university's sports and health complex, facilities for its nursing and midwifery courses, and resources for trainee teachers.

Universities across the UK say they are facing financial pressures, with the neighbouring University of Sussex looking to save £35m a year in May in proposals to cut 200 jobs.

Its vice-chancellor, Prof Sasha Roseneil, said "very difficult decisions" were needed to "address the financial sustainability crisis affecting UK higher education".

title: McConnell’s return shines spotlight on older lawmakers
description: Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) expected return to the Senate next week is drawing attention again to the health of aging lawmakers. McConnell, 84, was hospitalized over the summer for nearly two month...
fullText:
Sen. Mitch McConnell's (R-Ky.) expected return to the Senate next week is drawing attention again to the health of aging lawmakers.

McConnell, 84, was hospitalized over the summer for nearly two months after falling at home and receiving treatment for pneumonia. He has since been recovering at home and engaging in what he described as an "intensive regimen of physical therapy."

His extended absence and advanced age have reignited conversations about lawmakers staying in office too long, with polls showing many voters support term limits, even as they also keep reelecting elder statesmen.

McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1985 and is the 10th longest-serving senator in U.S. history. He is not seeking reelection to his current term, which ends in January.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) has repeatedly raised questions over whether McConnell is fit to serve because of his health challenges this summer.

"I hope that he is one of the reasons that we get term limits. I'll tell you what, I'd even name the bill after him," Beshear told CNN.

Iowa's 44-year-old Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Rob Sand, has voiced his support for both age and term limits.

"The idea is, I want term limits. I want age limits. Let's go get them," he told reporters in April.

Compounding these arguments is the recent spate of lawmakers who have died in office — six in this term alone. Democratic Reps. Raúl Grijalva (Ariz.), Gerry Connolly (Va.) and David Scott (Ga.) were a decade or more past the typical retirement age of 65. Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.) was 71 when he died in office from aortic dissection — a sudden condition that is not typically screened for — in July.

In 2023, 90-year-old Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) died while in office.

Rep. Kay Granger (R-Texas) had left office less than two years before her death last month at age 83. The end of her tenure was marred by the revelation that she had been residing in a senior living facility and experiencing what her son Brandon Granger described at the time as "dementia issues." Her family confirmed her death was caused by complications from Alzheimer's disease.

Support for term limits on Congress remains overwhelmingly popular among Americans across the political spectrum.

An NPR/PBS News/Marist poll released in May found that 83 percent of U.S. adults support term limits, with self-identified Republicans showing the highest rate of support at 89 percent. The same survey found that 80 percent of Americans also support an age cap on congressional candidates.

According to Aaron Dukette, senior strategist for the nonpartisan advocacy group U.S. Term Limits, support for imposing term limits has "skyrocketed" among Congress members in the past few years.

"We have 130-plus people who have signed a pledge and gotten on as co-sponsors for our amendment. So, it's not obviously at the two-thirds threshold that you need to have both chambers, but it's certainly growing," Dukette told The Hill. "And I think people on both sides of the aisle started to recognize that this is something that's going to benefit our whole electoral process and not just one party over the other."

The joint resolution supported by his organization proposes limiting U.S. senators to two terms and House members to three terms. The version introduced in the House last year has 115 co-sponsors, 107 of whom are Republicans.

Although conversations and support for term limits and age limits persist among the general public, the discussions are rarer among lawmakers themselves, according to those who've worked with them.

Rodney Whitlock, managing director of Cozen O'Connor Public Strategies, was health policy adviser to Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) until 2015. Grassley, who will turn 93 next week, is now the oldest member of Congress and was among the oldest when Whitlock last worked for him more than a decade ago. Grassley ranks as the longest-serving U.S. senator currently in the chamber, exceeding McConnell's tenure by four years.

"It is not as common as one would think, unless the member starts to have issues," Whitlock said when asked whether lawmakers and their staff talk about age.

He argued that the issue of an aging workforce is a broad one.

"Nobody should be looking at this going, 'This is a unique problem to members of Congress.' No, it's not. It is societal. It is our issues with aging. All of these things are part of this conversation," said Whitlock. He noted that during his time as a congressional staffer, views on aging lawmakers were more respectful, but the discussions have since become "overtly political."

While describing that Grassley sees public service as a "calling," Whitlock said there are "certainly" lawmakers who stay in office simply because they have "grown so accustomed to the lifestyle."

Discussions about American gerontocracy encompass all branches of government. President Trump, 80, is the oldest person to be sworn in as U.S. president; former President Biden became the oldest sitting president, leaving office at 82.

At the Supreme Court, 5 out of 8 sitting justices are past age 65; Justice Clarence Thomas is the oldest at 78.

Dukette from U.S. Term Limits said his organization is focused on limiting congressional service based on terms over age, reasoning that limiting terms would naturally resolve the age issue.

"We understand the concern and the desire for age limits, given the fact that we have many prominent elderly members of Congress that are running into health troubles while still being in office and they go ... missing for a time," said Dukette. "If it wasn't for the 20, 30, 40-year careers that put them in that place in the first place — most members that run for Congress don't start doing so in their 60s or 70s. They do so in their 40s or even in their 50s, and then they're there for decades of service."

When reached for comment on his condition and expected return, McConnell's office referred to the senator's last public statement released at the start of August, in which he said he would "continue my recovery at home" and "continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business."

The Hill has reached out to Grassley's office for comment.

title: Major companies to cut back on 2027 health benefits in blow to workers
description: Disney and Starbucks are among firms cutting health benefits for 2027 as medical costs continue to soar. This trend may mean you'll pay more.
fullText:
Health benefits are a top factor in whether Americans take or stay in a job, yet in a span of a few weeks, a handful of large employers reportedly are planning cutbacks or changes that can make that choice even tougher in 2027.

Walt Disney, Bloomberg, Starbucks, Deloitte, and the City of Dallas are among those taking actions next year to rein in health care spending, from restricting spousal coverage to eliminating plan options or cutting drug benefits to deal with soaring costs. Health plans are projecting the highest medical cost trend in nearly two decades, with commercial health care costs expected to rise 9% in 2027, according to consulting firm PwC. Insurer Aon predicted even higher costs, with U.S. employer health care costs increasing 9.5% next year, pushing average costs above $19,000 per employee.

These benefit cuts could be devastating for workers if they have to shoulder more of their own health costs, analysts said. Americans already say they have limited budgets for health insurance outside an employer-sponsored plan, according to finance researcher ValuePenguin. Overall, 42% of the 2,001 adults surveyed in July said they could comfortably afford less than $100 a month, while 23% said they could afford between $100 and $249.

"Health insurance is much more than a minor perk for most working Americans," said Maggie Gunara, senior staff writer at ValuePenguin, in a report. "Among those who are employed or job hunting, 87% say the health plan attached to a job matters at least somewhat when they're deciding whether to take a job or stick around."

Some of the companies making cuts include:

Walt Disney Co. will stop covering working spouses under its health care plan in 2027 if those spouses have access to coverage through their own employers. The change applies to the company's more than 200,000 U.S. employees.

Starbucks surprised workers when open enrollment began by nearly doubling the price tag for health insurance for some workers and lowering the share of employer contribution to the cost. It's also ending coverage for GLP-1 weight loss drugs, beginning in October.

Bloomberg LP plans to make its employees start paying monthly premium contributions for the first time in the company's history.

Deloitte will halve paid parental leave to eight weeks for workers in its "Center" talent segment, which covers internal IT, finance, and administrative functions, effective Jan. 1. It's also ending for those workers its $50,000 adoption and surrogacy reimbursement program, which also covered IVF-related costs, as well as pension accruals after Dec. 31.

The Dallas City Council will vote on Sept. 16 on a proposal to eliminate its copay insurance plan and end GLP-1 coverage for employees using the medication for weight loss.

title: Africa's top health body warns Congo’s Ebola outbreak is rapidly spreading beyond epicenter
description: The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record in eastern Congo is rapidly spreading beyond its epicenter, Africa’s top health body said Thursday.  In recent weeks, new cases and deaths have declined in...
fullText:
KINSHASA, Congo (AP) — The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record in eastern Congo is rapidly spreading beyond its epicenter, Africa's top health body said Thursday.

In recent weeks, new cases and deaths have declined in Ituri province, the outbreak's epicenter, but risen sharply in neighboring North Kivu and Haut-Uele, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said at a weekly briefing.

According to the latest government figures released on Thursday, 6,843 cases have been reported, including 3,310 deaths. Ituri province remains the hardest-hit province, with more than 5,400 cases while North Kivu has reported over 1,000 cases since the outbreak was declared in May.

The outbreak in eastern Congo is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers' strike and intense population movements. The situation is particularly concerning at displacement sites, where residents already live in extremely precarious conditions.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

In North Kivu, new cases more than doubled to 381 in the latest three-week period, from 165 in the earlier period, Yap Boum, Africa CDC's head of emergency preparedness and response, said Thursday.

The virus recently reached two more health zones in North Kivu, where fighting between government forces and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels, who control the provincial capital Goma, has complicated the response.

Last month, Congo began vaccinating health and other front-line workers with the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type called Zaire.

Clinical trials are underway to find a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo virus.

The vaccination trials started in the eastern Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele provinces, Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC's director for research, clinical trials and innovation, said Thursday.

Kingebeni said the vaccination campaign initially targeted newly affected provinces to help prevent further spread. Vaccinations in Ituri are set to start next week, he added.

A key challenge is the limited supply of doses, said Kingebeni. Congo has received 70,000 doses so far.

Banchereau reported from Dakar, Senegal.

title: You Don't Need the Apple Watch 12 to Get All the New Health Features
description: Some features require the newest Apple Watch, but others will work on the watch or phone you already have.
fullText:
Apple recently announced some big changes to the Health app, as well as new sensors in the upcoming Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. The company bundled these and other health-related announcements together, but that doesn't mean you need an Apple Watch 12 to take advantage of all the new features. Here's the breakdown of which Apple Watches will get the new features—and which ones don't need an Apple Watch at all.

You'll need the new Series 12 or the Ultra 4 to get Apple's new heart rate sensor—the one it's billing as the most accurate in any wearable. (Huge if true.) These two watches also have the new S11 processing chip. The sensor and the chip are required for what Apple is calling its "health sensing system," which gives you more frequent heart rate and HRV readings throughout the day.

According to Apple, the new systems measure heart rate every five seconds instead of every five minutes, and HRV every five minutes instead of every few hours. Overnight vitals will now include a Recovery HRV score that's compared to your baseline (so you know when your body is under more or less stress than usual). The Readiness score seems to rely on these readings, so you'll need one of the new watches to get that score.

I recently wrote about the changes Apple has planned for the new Health app and noted that those are likely to be software changes that don't require a new phone or watch. Apple writes in a footnote on the Apple Watch page that the redesigned Health app requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (or iPad). The full list of Apple Intelligence-enabled devices is here, and they include the iPhone 15 Pro and all iPhones 16 and newer.

The new app includes "insights," which seem to be similar to the trends you'll see in the current Apple Health app. If you've ever noticed the little cards that say things like "your cardio fitness has been trending up for 8 weeks," it seems we'll get more of those, and they'll be collected together into their own area of the app. There will also be text summaries of your data and recommendations for what to do next, apparently written by Apple Intelligence based on your data.

The new Health app includes an on-demand VO2max test you can do indoors. Apple's event video showed a person propping up their phone on the floor, making sure the phone's camera could see their entire body, and then following along with a metronome by stepping in place on the beat. You'll need a heart rate sensor to do this test and get your results, and Apple says that any Apple Watch will do—or AirPods Pro 3, or a third-party sensor.

In other words, it sounds like it can work with any device that broadcasts heart rate, which includes just about any wearable out there. If you have a Fitbit, a Whoop, or a Garmin (to name a few), you can probably get it to broadcast your heart rate and thus work with this test. Apple's Fitness app can already read heart rate from these devices, so I expect the compatibility to be the same for the VO2max test.

Workout Buddy, which takes the form of a motivational voice in your ear during workouts, requires Apple Intelligence. Previously, this meant you needed to carry an Apple Intelligence-enabled phone with you during workouts, but that's changing. The new Workout Buddy can work from your Apple Watch without needing a phone, so long as your watch has access to the Internet through either cellular data or a wifi network (such as your gym's wifi). Compatible watches include the Series 9 and newer, the Ultra 2 and later, or the Apple Watch SE 3.

title: I was a working mom at Amazon who struggled to relax. After I was laid off, I went all in on wellness.
description: Rania Zheng struggled to relax while juggling motherhood and a career at Amazon. After her layoff, she went all in on her wellness-travel business.
fullText:
Rania Zheng struggled to relax while working at Amazon, so she sought out holistic wellness practices.

She was laid off in October 2025 and turned her wellness interest into a full-time business.

Rania's business offers curated trips in China focusing on different wellness themes.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rania Zheng, a 34-year-old former senior technical product manager at Amazon living in Bellevue, Washington. Zheng was laid off from Amazon in October 2025 and now runs her own wellness-travel business. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

When I learned last October that I was being laid off from Amazon after nearly six years, I was surprised. However, it didn't feel like the end of the world.

Layoffs had become common across the tech industry. I'd heard stories from friends who had been impacted at other companies. I also didn't feel like I was being targeted or that the decision was about my performance.

My official separation from the company only took effect in January, so I had time to pause and think about what I wanted at this stage of my life.

I could look for another job. Or, instead, I could spend more time on the side project I'd already started while working at Amazon. Losing my job gave me a push to see whether I could focus full-time on turning that early idea into an actual business.

I joined Amazon in 2020 as a business intelligence engineer, shortly before the pandemic began. About a year later, I was promoted to a senior engineer.

I'd taken product management classes at the University of Washington and let my managers know I wanted to explore more work in that area. They were supportive, and in 2022, I transitioned into a senior product manager role.

Overall, my experience at Amazon was very positive. I felt like I could continue challenging myself and exploring what I wanted to do.

However, as a woman in a competitive workplace, it could be hard to balance work, my husband, my children, and the invisible mental load. People would tell me that I should relax more, but I didn't really know how.

Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form, emailing him, or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here.

My efforts to relax more eventually led me to explore holistic wellness, including traditional Chinese medicine, tea practices, and Qigong. I found it very helpful, and thought more people should know about them.

So, early last year, I cofounded my wellness-travel business, Puyu Retreat, which offers curated trips of roughly five to seven days in China. Depending on the destination, the trips cover different wellness themes.

One trip, for example, focuses on tea and traditional Chinese medicine, while another destination focuses more on creative mindfulness.

At first, the business was more of an idea I was testing with my cofounder, who is based in China. I mostly worked on things like our social media posts about our destinations and the cultural side of the business. I spent around two to three hours a week on the business alongside my Amazon job.

Our first retreat ran in November 2025 — the month after I was laid off.

We've since run some tours, are generating revenue, and the business is growing steadily. Our Instagram account has grown to over 20,000 followers. My cofounder and a founding member now lead our operations on the ground in China. Overall, I'm optimistic about our progress.

Still, I'm not paying myself from the business yet. We're not yet profitable, and we're reinvesting everything into the trips themselves. Each retreat is designed for a small group and is hand-curated, so a significant amount of time and attention goes into each one. Our next focus is on growing in the US market.

One of the reasons I felt comfortable pursuing the business is that my husband works, we have savings to fall back on, and our family isn't spending a lot right now. That gives us some financial runway, but I know this might not make sense forever.

When I decided to focus more seriously on the business, I gave myself roughly a year from when I was laid off to see whether it kept showing promise. If not, I could consider returning to the job market.

As the one-year mark gets closer, I find myself more and more drawn to work that leans into my strengths, such as creativity, sharp business instinct, and translating data into actionable insights.

Building the business draws on all of these skills, but I know other roles could as well. While I'm not actively looking for work right now, I've kept an eye on the market. I wouldn't rule out interviewing if the right opportunity came along and aligned with what I do best.

When I started exploring wellness practices, my goal was to relax more. Since leaving Amazon, building a wellness business has been stressful in its own ways — but when you're working on something you genuinely care about, that changes the quality of the stress.

Working on the business has also helped me keep up with my wellness practices because I have to practice what I'm selling. I've gotten deeper into traditional Chinese medicine and have really come to appreciate its holistic view of health.

Overall, I'm focused on building a balance between work and life that actually holds.

One of the biggest things I've learned about building a business is not to build in silence. There are a lot of ways to validate whether your idea is promising; you can talk to people you trust, share on social media, and see whether people respond.

I'd also tell people who've been laid off not to take it personally. A layoff isn't the end of the story, and everything you accumulated in your previous roles is still valuable.

I appreciate all the experience I gained in product analytics, business intelligence, and product management. It taught me about technology, how to scale, and how to prioritize things.

Those skills don't disappear after a layoff. They can help you figure out what comes next.
