fullText:
Prince William has urged sport at every level to make suicide prevention part of its culture through a new nationwide toolkit.

Launched by the Prince of Wales and the Royal Foundation, On Your Side, external is a set of resources available online that aims "to make suicide prevention as much a part of sport as warm-up, training and performance".

The project is backed by more than 70 organisations including the Football Association, Premier League, Team GB, British Cycling and a host of leading mental health charities.

"Through my work on mental health, I have met people whose lives have been changed forever by suicide," said Prince William. "But I have also met people whose lives have been saved because someone stepped in to help."

The 44-year-old Royal, who has previously spoken about his own struggles with mental health issues, said that while he acknowledges the good work being done by current services, too often "initiatives are fragmented" and "support is inconsistent, particularly at a grassroots level".

William added that he hopes On Your Side provides everyone involved in sport who notices someone is struggling the "clear, practical guidance" to help that person find the support they need.

On Your Side is being launched to coincide with World Suicide Prevention Day on 10 September.

William says it has taken 'long time to understand my emotions'

According to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), there were 6,190 suicides registered in England and Wales in 2024.

It remains the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 and the rate remains notably higher among males (17.6 per 100,000 people) than females (5.7 per 100,000).

The toolkit will officially be launched at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium, a venue chosen because its construction included a 'talking bench' in memory of former player Gary Speed.

Ex-Wales captain and manager Speed, who also played for Leeds, Bolton, Newcastle and Sheffield United, took his own life in November 2011.

Premier League record goalscorer and Match of the Day pundit Alan Shearer, who was a close friend of Speed, is among the athletes to have given their backing to the initiative.

"For me, this is obviously very personal," said Shearer.

"We can't always know when somebody is struggling, but we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support.

"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers, but I hope that everyone in sport will use the toolkit."

Prince William said he wants On Your Side to take advantage of sport's "remarkable ability to bring people together".

He added: "In moments of need, the right support can make all the difference. We all have the power to help, and that's why suicide prevention must be an important part of everyday sporting life."

The National Health Service, the Samaritans and mental health charity Mind were all consulted during the creation of On Your Side.

The Royal Foundation said the project had taken two years to complete and added that, although it was being launched to coincide with World Suicide Prevention Day, the initiative is "not a one-day campaign" and hopes it will have a long-lasting legacy.

title: Why the Apple Health App's Redesign Is a Big Deal
description: We've needed this dashboard for years.
fullText:
Apple announced new watches today—a Series 12 and an Ultra 4—which you can read more about here. But alongside the watch features, Apple announced a revamped Health app. We’ll soon have a proper dashboard for health data and insights, rivaling what you can get from the companion apps for other wearables like Whoop, Garmin, and Fitbit.

Apple was an early trendsetter when it came to health-focused watches, but it quickly fell behind as all the other devices began adding sleep scores, recovery scores, and customized insights based on your day’s data. If you open up a good wearable app, you’ll instantly know what’s going on with your body’s data and what you should probably do about it. I’m often skeptical of the specifics—you shouldn’t read too much into any app’s metrics—but it’s good to have something to look at.

The Apple Health app has existed for years, but it’s mostly a dry listing of data from different sources. Which is a shame, because it has access to an incredible amount of data, not to mention powerful hidden features that most of us never manage to discover.

Last year, Apple finally revamped its Fitness app to match what other wearables give us in terms of activity tracking. This year, we finally get the other half: a Health app that can tell you how well you slept, how “recovered” you are, and how your long-term health seems to be shaping up.

Although Apple showed these features in the context of an Apple Watch upgrade (more on that below), the things that intrigue me most are likely to be software updates that roll out to iPhones in general. That’s my guess, in any case—I’ll watch Apple’s announcements 

Apple showed a new Readiness score, which can tell you whether you need to “recover,” should “pace yourself,” are “ready,” or should “go for it.” (That’s in order from worst to best.) This score can update during the day, making it a more readable version of something like Garmin’s Body Battery.

When you open your Health app, it looks like relevant “insights” will show up at the top of the screen, including your sleep, recovery, and rings, and the main screen can show your sleep from the past night along with a sleep score. The app includes text summaries and guidance that are generated by Apple Intelligence, suggesting that you'll need an iPhone 16 or later for these.

In the screenshots Apple shared, I spied a tiny number that is actually a huge change of focus for the company: one of the insights shows your rings next to your step count for the day. Apple has never made a big deal about steps, to the point where people often download third-party step counters to be able to easily view steps on the watch. But the Health app has kept count all along, and now that number is showing up somewhere you can easily see it.

Depending on how well Apple executes this idea, I could see apps like Bevel becoming obsolete. And Bevel already makes some wearables’ apps (like Google Health) obsolete—you can just read the data from Bevel, or now Apple Health, instead of using the app that comes with your Fitbit. Other fitness tech companies will now have a serious competitor that is available for free on customers’ phones.

I roll my eyes every time a health or fitness app claims to gauge my “longevity” or some true “age” of my body. Depending on which app you ask, I’m either 10 years younger than I really am, or three years older.

Apple has joined the club, with a whole Longevity tab in the Health app. (That now brings the number of tabs to three: the main screen, the sharing tab, and now longevity in the middle.) Despite the eye-rolling, I see what Apple is doing here. Don’t think of longevity in this (or any) app as being an accurate gauge of how long you will live; think of it as how your long-term health habits are adding up. Apple’s longevity calculations involve seven areas, with icons indicating something like nutrition, exercise, heart health, hearing health, movement (maybe steps), sleep, and mental well-being.

There’s also a new set of assessments, including a VO2max assessment. According to Apple’s presentation, you’ll prop your phone up where it can see your full body, and then you’ll step to a metronome’s beat, speeding up as the beeps speed up until you’re running in place. This sounds like it may have been inspired by the Harvard step test, which has you step up and down in place and then measure your heart rate. Until now, Apple’s VO2max estimates have always been based on GPS-tracked activities like outdoor running. (Apple finished in the middle of the pack when I tested the accuracy of nine devices’ VO2max estimates. I’m curious to see whether the new assessment does better.)

When it comes to the full experience—with the Apple Watch itself—there’s a notable upgrade to the Series 12 Apple Watch compared to previous versions. Apple has redesigned the heart rate sensor on the back of the watch, with larger lights and redesigned photodiodes to detect the reflected light.

With these redesigns, Apple says it has the “most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” To which I say: I’ll believe it when I see it. In my testing over the past few years, Apple Watches have lagged well behind other wearables’ heart rate sensors when I test them for accuracy. I’d certainly believe that it found room for improvement, but is the new Apple sensor really going to be able to beat Garmin’s fifth-generation sensor, the one that made me do a double take because I thought I had it mixed up with my chest strap data?

Apple has released a whitepaper with the results of an internal heart rate accuracy study it did comparing the Series 12 (but not the Ultra 4) against the Garmin Forerunner 970, Google Pixel Watch 4, Huawei Watch 5, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, Whoop 5.0, and Oura Ring 5, with a Polar H10 chest strap for reference. It's a short paper, and doesn't show the kind of detail I would like to see from a thorough test, so you can bet I'll be investigating this myself once I get my hands on the new watch. If Apple really reaches a Forerunner 970 level of accuracy, I’ll be incredibly impressed.

title: Joe Biden shares health update after prostate cancer diagnosis while issuing warning to others
description: Joe Biden revealed his radiation treatment from last fall "worked as intended" as he urged men to discuss prostate cancer screening with their doctors.
fullText:
Former President Joe Biden shared an update on his battle with prostate cancer Tuesday, revealing that radiation treatment he underwent last fall "worked as intended" while urging American men not to delay conversations with their doctors about cancer screening.

Biden, 83, issued the update in a lengthy social media post marking Prostate Cancer Awareness Month, saying the occasion was more personal for him following his diagnosis last year.

"The radiation treatment from last fall worked as intended, and I continue to do the things I care about, like finishing my memoir," Biden wrote.

Jill Biden Says Former President Will Live With Stage 4 Cancer 'For The Rest Of His Life,' Has Slowed Down

He also thanked the doctors, nurses and other medical professionals who have treated him, saying their "skill, dedication, and compassion mean so much."

Biden used much of the message to urge men to discuss prostate cancer screening with their doctors, pointing to the dramatically higher survival rate when the disease is detected early.

Cancer Treatment Delays Surge Across Us As Doctor Warns System 'Needs Fixing Immediately'

"Talk to your doctors. Ask the hard questions. Do it for yourself, and do it for the people who love you," Biden wrote.

Biden said men at average risk should begin discussing prostate cancer screening with their doctors around age 50, while Black men and those with a family history should begin those conversations earlier.

Simple Sitting Change Linked To Lower Risk Of Cancer Death, Study Finds

The American Cancer Society recommends discussing screening at age 50 for average-risk men, age 45 for Black men and certain men with a family history, and age 40 for some men at even higher risk.

Biden's office announced in May 2025 that the former president had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had metastasized to his bones.

The diagnosis came after Biden experienced increasing urinary symptoms and doctors discovered a prostate nodule. His office said at the time that the cancer had a Gleason score of 9, Grade Group 5, but was hormone-sensitive, allowing for effective management.

Biden later underwent radiation therapy and completed that course of treatment last fall.

Fox News Digital reached out to Biden's office for additional comment on his current health, treatment and prognosis.

Biden closed Tuesday's message by thanking those who have continued to pray for him and his family.

"It's my hope and prayer that by sharing our experience and being part of this important conversation, we can help save lives," he wrote. "And no matter what, keep the faith. God bless you."

fullText:
This column is usually filled with bad takes, daft footballing opinion and poor attempts at humour, but today I want to be a little more serious.

The gaffer, Jim Goodwin, is going through a health issue at present. And for his own and his family's sake, I hope he can return to full health as soon as possible.

As a player, Goodwin was never my favourite, in fact, he likely wasn't anyone's favourite. For a start, he was always in the opposition, but I'll concede, he played the game in an honest and often robust manner.

He'd tell you himself he wasn't the best player to pull on a pair of boots, but he made the most of 'what he had'. That in itself is admirable.

Since becoming Dundee United manager, it's been clear to see he's a passionate, amiable, well-spoken, determined, thoughtful and proud man, who has represented our club wonderfully well and given his absolute all.

Through no fault of his own, he's had to build four teams in his time at Tannadice. With those teams he has achieved, I would imagine, most of what was asked of him, albeit this season is still in its infancy.

He has fronted up every week, regardless of result, and taken the full force of flak and blame when there are also others at fault when things haven't gone well. Yes, I'm looking at you lot upstairs.

Far be it from me to speculate what Goodwin is going through, but he and every other manager in the league must experience some amount of stress on a near daily basis.

Yes, football managers are in a relatively privileged position, but we need to remember they are human. They have good days, they have difficult days. They also suffer from ill health at times, and when that happens, football tends to pale into insignificance.

So from myself and many, many others, I wish you well, Jim. Haste ye back to health and the dugout.

title: Why getting your hands dirty is good for you
description: Putting our hands in soil and touching grass, trees or moss provides a wide range of health benefits, for our skin and wider immune system.
fullText:
Putting our hands in soil and touching grass, trees or moss provides a wide range of health benefits, for our skin and wider immune system.

I take a long walk in my nearest park every day, almost religiously. There are plenty of different tree species to look at, an everchanging cast of fragrant flowers in spring, and enthusiastic birdsong fills the air. But the sensory experience usually stops there. However mucky my shoes get, I usually come home with clean hands.

Research, though, suggests there's something to be said for reaching out to touch the trees, shrubs and soil I usually walk past. Mira Grönroos, an ecologist and nature-health researcher at the Finnish Environment Institute, asked people to rub their hands with soil, peat and moss for 20 seconds as part of an experiment. She found that the abundance and variety of microbes on their skin increased, even after they rinsed their hands with tap water. "To the naked eye [their hands] looked clean," she says, "but the change was so huge".

The idea of more bacteria on our skin might not sound appealing. But when there's a rich mix of microbes living alongside each other, they keep each other in check and defend us against more harmful, pathogenic bacteria. A growing body of research shows that contact with natural materials, like soil and plants, is an easy way to boost our skin's microbial diversity, and that this not only benefits our skin, but also our immune system.

Twenty seconds isn't long – I'd happily pause on my walk to touch some tree bark or sit down in the grass. But more would be much better, Grönroos says, as in her experiment "the skin microbiota very quickly returned to a similar state as it was before". The results suggest that prolonged or frequent skin contact with nature could significantly change what's happening on our skin and in our bodies.

Mucky hands are the norm for children at Aurinkolinna daycare centre in central Finland. They spend at least a couple of hours every day playing outside in a wooded playground, racing between bushes and trees, climbing ropes, making sandcastles, splashing in puddles and grabbing fistfuls of dirt and woodchips.

Aurinkolinna is one of 43 daycare centres in Finland taking part in the Vahvistu research project, which builds on a recent two-year study led by environmental scientist Marja Roslund.

In 2016-17, she brought the forest floor into a daycare yard – complete with peat and planting boxes – and measured the impact on young children's skin, saliva and gut bacteria after they had played there regularly for 28 days, and again after a year. Compared to children who played in a paved yard, those on the forest floor had greater microbial diversity on their skin a year later.

This diversity is important for the health of our skin. Increasing the diversity of bacteria on the skin can prevent disease-causing bacteria from becoming dominant, keeping the microbial community in balance, Roslund says. "Disease is like a dictator, and healthy skin is like a democracy."

Roslund's research found fewer potential pathogens on children's skin when they had played on the forest floor, likely because the number and diversity of other microbes crowds out these "bad" bacteria. "Because there is so much of everything else, there is not so much space for the pathogens," she says.

Taking care of our skin also has benefits that run much deeper. Skin health can impact hormonal activity, cardiovascular disease, and even cognitive function. In particular, research is starting to show that exposing our skin to diverse bacteria can impact our immune system.

Roslund asked a group of young children to play in a sandbox enriched with microbially diverse soil, while another group played in a sandbox that looked the same but contained less microbial diversity. As we might expect, the diversity of certain bacteria on children's skin increased when they played in the microbially rich sandbox. But there were also changes to the immune markers, called cytokines, in these children's blood samples that support immunoregulation – the immune system's ability to fight off threats without becoming overactive.

It is these and similar findings that inspired the Vahvistu project. At Aurinkolinna, government funding has helped transform the yard so it now includes woodchips instead of gravel, a bigger sanded area, and wooden pathways, alongside the birch and pine trees that were already there.

The research behind the Vahvistu project supports what is known as the biodiversity hypothesis – the idea that air, plants and soil rich in diverse microbes have an important influence on the human microbiome, and therefore our health. It has long been suggested that the loss of biodiversity in our environment could be behind the current rise in immune-related conditions, and Roslund's research may help to explain how and why that is.

She found that one family of bacteria, namely gammaproteobacteria, plays a particularly important role. Gammaproteobacterial diversity increased on children's skin when they played in the yard with the forest floor, and this increase was associated with more regulatory T cells – white blood cells that help control and balance the immune system and are important for preventing autoimmune diseases, she says.

For now, it's not clear exactly what this means for immune-mediated diseases like eczema, asthma or allergies. "We cannot yet say that when you have contact with nature, you will not get asthma, for example. But it seems that it might reduce the possibility of getting those immune system disorders," Grönroos says.

These health benefits aren't only seen in children. In one study, adults were asked to grow vegetables indoors over winter, some using microbially diverse soil and others using similar-looking but microbially poor soil. They tended to the plants every day for a month and ate their crops. Those using the microbially-diverse soil saw an increase in the diversity of bacteria on their skin, and on the number of anti-inflammatory cytokines in their blood – while the other group didn't.

This kind of gardening "is a good example of an easily accessible way of nature contact, and it was quite surprising that this kind of exposure really showed changes in the immune system functioning", Grönroos says.

In another study, researchers installed "green walls" made of living plants in Finnish offices and measured the effect on workers after two weeks. They found that the diversity of microbes on their skin increased, and levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in their blood went down. They also saw an increase in Lactobacillus microbes on their skin, which is important for skin health.

• Four benefits of going out in the rain

• Want a better night's sleep? Go camping

• What watching the sunset really does for your health

Grönroos puts her findings into practice with her own family. "When I go outdoors with my children, if they want to pick some cones or sticks, I don't say 'no' to them. I let them bring them home and play there."

We should start applying this thinking to our cities, Grönroos adds. "[Cities] should be built so that citizens are able to get into contact with nature. It would be good if some of that contact was unintentional, so people wouldn't need to decide to go there, they would come into contact with nature on their way to work or school," she says.

There's more for science to discover about exactly how contact with nature impacts the immune system, but for Grönroos, the findings so far are enough to make the grubby hands and muddy carpet worth it. "It's low risk," she says, with "lots of potential benefits without any obvious major harms."

These findings are, perhaps, a reminder to us all to reach out and touch that mossy tree, to sit down in the grass – to not be afraid of a bit of mud.

fullText:
James Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outs

Concern is being raised about Palantir’s work with the NHS as new figures showed tens of thousands of patients have withdrawn their data from use in research projects.

James Frith, the health innovation minister, said he was worried about “mistrust” of the US defence and health tech company and “the impact it could have on people’s willingness to share data with the NHS”.

The government is deciding whether to axe the company’s £330m contract to operate the health service’s federated data platform, which is intended to improve efficiency and patient outcomes.

Frith’s comment, in a letter to Layla Moran, the chair of the Commons health committee, follows a rise in patients opting out of allowing their medical data to be shared. In the two months from mid-May to mid-July, 60,000 more people withdrew their private information under a mechanism called the national data opt-out.

Doctors and patients’ groups are calling for Labour to exercise a break clause in Palantir’s seven-year contract. They cite its work with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration agency and question the company’s claim to provide value for money.

Palantir and its supporters say its AI-driven technology has cut NHS waiting lists for surgery. A spokesperson for the company said it was “helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 110,000 additional operations, a 15% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 6.8% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days”.

NHS England has reported similar numbers but said it could not “draw conclusions about cause and effect”. The government’s statistics watchdog is investigating the data.

Frith told Moran there had been an increase in NHS data opt-outs, in line with media interest in Palantir’s position.

Palantir’s government contracts have been beset by controversy. Ministers apologised after it emerged that the company’s staff had access to identifiable patient data.

London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has also blocked the Metropolitan police from awarding Palantir a £50m contract to use its AI to support investigations. He said Londoners wanted to see public money paid only to companies that “share the values of our city”. Palantir is suing over the mayor’s decision.

Frith said the rise in opt-outs was “modest” but would still be monitored. Opting out does not stop an individual’s records from being used for direct care, such as live operations. However, it prevents it being used for research and planning.

Frith said: “It may not be possible to realise the benefits of the 10-year health plan if patients stop sharing their data.”

Foxglove, a tech equity campaign, welcomed the minister’s acknowledgment of apparent public mistrust of Palantir. “Doctors and patients have been warning about the threat this poses to NHS care, and tens of thousands of people have opted out in just the last few months,” said Tom Hegarty, its head of communications.

“People are right to be concerned given … its founder, Trump ally Peter Thiel, going on record to opine that the NHS makes people sick.”

Frith indicated a policy shift on whether the Palantir-powered platform must be used by NHS trusts. In July, a health minister told parliament that health trusts would be told they “must use” parts of NHS England’s federated platform, which is controlled using Palantir technology. Now Frith has said “there is no requirement to use the FDP” and they may “prefer an alternative”.

Moran, who is a Liberal Democrat MP, said she welcomed the “softened stance” on whether adoption of the FDP was mandatory but added: “We remain of the view that the government should switch provider and not extend the current contract. Given how long this process could take, ministers need to act decisively and quickly, and not put this decision off until February.”

title: Socialism 2026 speaker slams diet industry for policing 'Black fat flesh,' calls it 'body fascism'
description: A Socialism 2026 speaker argued that policing "Black fat flesh" anchors entire systems of governance, calling modern health standards body fascism.
fullText:
An activist at the Socialism 2026 conference in Chicago slammed the "diet industry" for policing "Black fat flesh," characterizing modern health standards and weight management as forms of "body fascism".

During a session on "Health Fascism" on Saturday, author Da'Shaun L. Harrison said that the policing of "Black fat flesh" is foundational to broader "entire systems of governance."

"Black fatness is made meaningful through suffering, through surveillance, and through control and the policing of Black fat flesh anchors entire systems of governance. Without a population to discipline, there would be no BMI, no obesity epidemic, and no medical or scientific institutions organized around managing fatness," Harrison said.

"The diet industry reflects this logic. It operates through what I once defined as formal and informal relationships among major food corporations, the medical-industrial complex, and individual wealthy benefactors to sustain a social order in which fat people are monitored, restricted, guilted, stolen from, and punished. Diet culture has always linked food to morality, framing restraint as virtue and pleasure as danger through language like 'guilty pleasure,'" Harrison said.

Democratic Socialists Erupt Over 2028 Endorsement As Aoc Speculation Grows: 'Dangerous Path'

The four-day Socialism 2026 conference, held at the Hyatt Regency McCormick Place and organized by Haymarket Books, brought together activists, organizers, and communities from across the country and around the world, featuring over a hundred participatory discussions, lectures, and workshops, according to the event's website.

Harrison was one of three panelists — alongside podcast co-hosts Beatrice Adler-Bolton and Artie Vierkant—who spoke during a session titled "Health Fascism, Body Politics, and the Anti-State State". Over 200 people attended the discussion, which formed part of the conference's broader "Health Fascism" series. Clips of the conference were shared on X by Manhattan Institute investigative analyst Stu Smith.

"As governments retreat from care, and health increasingly becomes a signifier of discipline—rather than provision—fitness, disability, fatness, illness, Blackness, impairment, and bodily capacity are mobilized into measures of moral worth and political belonging. title: Parents of San Diego mosque gunman say a mental health facility failed to heed FBI warning
description: Just days before two teenagers carried out a mass shooting at a San Diego mosque, federal law enforcement officials warned the parents of one of the shooters that their son was making concerning comme...
fullText:
Just days before two teenagers carried out a mass shooting at a San Diego mosque, federal law enforcement officials warned the parents of one of the shooters that their son was making concerning comments about school shootings on the dark web, according to new details included in a recently filed lawsuit.

The mother of Caleb Vazquez alleges in her lawsuit that Park Mental Health Treatment of San Diego failed to intervene despite signs that her 18-year-old son posed an imminent threat to himself and others. Vazquez was living there and receiving treatment for a range of mental health conditions, including depression and psychotic episodes, the lawsuit says. The court filings follow a number of high-profile convictions of guardians who provided teenagers with weapons that were later used in mass shootings.

The FBI called Vazquez's mother on the evening of May 14, and she said she immediately left a message with the treatment facility to notify its staff, according to the lawsuit, filed in a San Diego court on Aug. 31. Vazquez's mother again shared the FBI's warnings with her son's therapist on May 15 and with a program director later that night.

On May 18, the morning of the shooting, employees at the facility contacted Vazquez's mother to tell her that he was missing. Video surveillance footage subsequently showed Vazquez leaving the property at 8 p.m. the night before.

Vazquez's parents were driving around looking for him on the morning of the shooting. Vazquez and another teenager killed three people at the San Diego mosque that day before taking their own lives.

It is unclear whether Vazquez was allowed to leave the previous evening or whether he broke facility rules by doing so. Park Mental Health offers a range of treatment options, some of which advertise 24-hour surveillance, while others provide more limited counseling.

The center did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment Saturday afternoon. In a previous statement to radio station KPBS, Park Mental Health disputed the assertions in the lawsuit.

"While it is understandable that his parents might seek to blame someone in their time of loss, this lawsuit is misguided in that neither Park nor its employees are responsible for Mr. Vazquez's actions," the statement to KPBS read. "Only he and his coconspirator bear responsibility for their conduct and, ultimately, his death."

An FBI spokesperson declined to comment Saturday, citing agency policy.

The FBI's alleged contact with Vazquez's parents was not the first sign of his mental deterioration.

Vazquez had been hospitalized for roughly three days in January 2026 after telling a classmate that he wanted to carry out a school shooting.

Almost exactly a year earlier, Vazquez was flagged to law enforcement for exhibiting alarming behavior and idolizing Nazis, prompting police to confiscate 26 guns from his father under a 2014 California law allowing firearms to be taken from people considered dangerous.

Authorities have said Vazquez met the other shooter, Cain Clark, 17, online and that both were radicalized there. Police have not shared more details about how they knew each other or specified whose weapons were used in the shooting.

The lawsuit was filed on the same day that North Carolina authorities announced the indictment of a 17-year-old in connection with the shooting.

title: Students divided over University of Michigan hiding first-semester grades for 2027 freshmen
description: University of Michigan students clash over a pass/fail policy hiding first-semester freshman grades, debating mental health relief versus study habits.
fullText:
ANN ARBOR, Mich. — University of Michigan students are split over a new administrative policy that will hide first-semester letter grades for incoming freshmen.

Some welcome the relief from academic pressure while others warn it could coddle students and fail to prepare them for the real world.

Starting in fall 2027, incoming first-year students enrolled in the university's College of Literature, Science, and the Arts (LSA) will have their first-semester transcript grades designated strictly as pass (P) or no credit (NC).

College Students Express Strong Trust In School Leaders Despite Broader Public Cynicism: Gallup

School officials say the pilot program aims to combat a growing "mental health crisis" on college campuses and ease the transition from high school to college.

"Our goal is to help first-year students acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys — core elements of a liberal arts and sciences education," the university stated in its announcement.

While students will still receive traditional letter grades and feedback directly from professors throughout the term, final marks will not appear on official external transcripts or factor into overall GPAs. The university will retain internal letter grade records for advising, financial aid eligibility, academic awards and scholarships and other administrative purposes.

Several students told Fox News Digital that easing into college expectations could be a net positive.

"If there are measures to ease the way for high school students coming to [college], I think that's a good thing," said Alexander, an exchange grad student from Austria.

Ella Langlois, an LSA student, said it does not hurt to give the policy a test run.

"I do think mental health is always super important," she said.

William Bushey, a civil engineering major, called the decision a "good call."

"I'm an engineer, so I go through all the weeder classes all the time," Bushey said. "There's a lot of successful people who struggle in their first-year classes but will just pass and then wind up being super successful later on."

Chloe Song, an economics freshman, agreed that the initial transition can be daunting.

"I think that's a good call because it's really stressful," Song said.

The LSA is the largest of the university's 19 schools and colleges, serving approximately 19,700 undergraduate students. University leaders hope the grade-covering policy gives students the freedom to explore challenging electives without fear of damaging their long-term GPAs.

Similar pass/fail or hidden-grade policies for first-year students have existed for decades at institutions such as Mit, Caltech, Wellesley and Swarthmore.

However, not all Michigan students are on board. Some argue that shielding grading consequences promotes poor study habits and ignores the root causes of student anxiety.

"I think it's kind of silly," said Talan, a freshman neuroscience major. "I know they say it's to curb mental health and stop people from having mental health crises, but I feel like that is our generation having access to media across the world. That's why their mental health is a little worse, not because they're worried about grades.

"We're at the University of Michigan. People tried pretty hard to get here," Talan added. "I feel like grades are taken pretty seriously. And if you're going to try, working as hard as someone who gets a C and passes with the same grade as you is kind of demeaning in a way."

Simran, a sophomore business major, suggested that hiding grades avoids teaching resilience.

"I think having more supportive resources is a better solution than hiding grades," Simran said. "I think there's a lot of challenges that you face in college, and challenging coursework is one of them. It's something you just learn to move through. I've definitely done poorly in classes before, but it's an upward battle at times. … It's a very important skill to have."

Others expressed concern the policy will merely delay academic stress until the second semester.

Andrew Spencer, a biology, health and society major, said that while he might have personally benefited from the break, he believes the policy will ultimately backfire.

"Overall, it's just going to hurt more," Spencer said. "People are just going to slack off and not care about their grades in the first semester and then not have the skills themselves for the second semester to come in and have a great work ethic."

Monica Diaz, a junior studying psychology and economics, offered a middle ground, noting that while she understands critics' concerns, the single-semester policy isn't permanent coddling.

"I don't entirely agree with that because I think it's just slowly transitioning them into what it's like to be at a school like the University of Michigan," Diaz said.

"Obviously, after the first semester, they're not going to be coddled anymore, so I don't really think that's entirely true. But I can definitely see the argument."

title: New York City pausing some AI tools in schools
description: New York City imposes a one-year moratorium on student-facing AI tools for grades K-8, citing concerns about youth mental health.
fullText:
“A six-year-old child is too young to slice an onion, to fry an egg or to use a stove safely. But once that child becomes 16, that knowledge becomes something they are mature enough to learn,” stressed New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani, while announcing a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students.

In what has been described as one of “the most expansive student-facing AI policies in the country”, the Mayor and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels on September 2 imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for pupils up to eighth grade for the 2026–27 academic year.

Here’s what you need to know about the moratorium, why NYC introduced it, and why the move could set a global precedent.

This move will affect nearly 6,00,000 public school students across the United States’ largest school district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, while the AI components of more than 38 previously approved programmes that fail to meet the new standards will be disabled or discontinued.

However, not all AI has been banned. Teachers can continue to use approved tools for planning and administrative work. Assistive technologies required by students with disabilities, as well as certain AI tools used in career-readiness programmes, remain permitted where necessary and under the policy’s safeguards.

Five limited AI pilots will also operate throughout the year for high school classrooms. These select tools are Quill (15 minutes per week) for English language arts; Edia (20 minutes per week) for mathematics; Brisk Teaching (10 to 20 minutes once or twice weekly) for teacher-created activities; Playlab (two assignments per marking period; 45 minutes per week) for assignment-specific applications; and Intel AI-Ready Schools (one period per week) to assist students in identifying community issues and developing solutions through term-long projects.

Every high school student will complete two 45-minute modules per year aimed at developing critical thinking around AI use, including its risks, limitations, and scope. Alongside AI restrictions, tighter individual screen-time limits have also been introduced. Children from 2-K through to second grade will have no routine screen time. For those in grades three to five, NYC Public Schools recommends no more than 30 minutes a day of individual screen use; for grades six to eight, the recommendation is 45 minutes. These restrictions do not prohibit teacher-led use of computers, tablets, or interactive whiteboards during lessons.

Throughout the academic year, a panel comprising students, educators, parents, elected officials, union partners, and field experts will assess the impact of the moratorium and pilots, delivering a report with policy recommendations in April 2027.

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow,” Mr. Mamdani said. “They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators, and wrestle with tough problems on their own.” Mr. Samuels also made a similar argument. Learning, he said, involves getting something wrong, trying again and eventually getting it right. That struggle is not an inconvenience that technology should eliminate; it is part of the learning process.

This move arrives amidst growing concern over screen time harming youth mental health. Studies have linked excessive scrolling, social media exposure and reliance on AI in children to lower critical thinking abilities, shorter attention spans, anxiety, and depression. While evidence connecting AI chatbots to suicide risk remains limited, several cases have prompted lawsuits alleging that interactions with chatbots contributed to young people’s deaths. Mr. Mamdani’s decision follows OpenAI’s launch of a teenage version of ChatGPT on August 18 featuring parental controls and content restrictions regarding self-harm and suicide. On August 26, Meta similarly announced stricter time limits, night-time blocking, and muted notifications during school hours for teenage accounts on Instagram and Facebook.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable but necessary. We do not see it that way,” Mr. Mamdani added.

Research supports a cautious stance. A 2026 CEPR discussion paper by researchers at Stockholm University and the University of Hong Kong examined more than 26,000 students in China over 30 months. They found that access to generative AI increased homework scores by 18% and reduced completion time by 30%. However, after roughly six months, the same students’ closed-book examination scores had fallen by 20%. A broader review by the Brookings Institution’s Centre for Universal Education, analysing over 400 studies and interviews with 500 educators and pupils across 50 countries, concluded that the potential harms of generative AI in primary and secondary education currently outweigh the benefits—though tailored applications with proper safeguards can enrich learning.

How are other parts of the world dealing with a similar dilemma? The United Arab Emirates is moving towards more structured AI education, rather than a moratorium. It has announced an AI curriculum across public and private schools covering areas such as data, algorithms, applications, risks and ethical use. It also plans to train about 22,000 educators in using AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis and lesson planning.

Norway has adopted a more cautious approach. Its education authorities have recommended that pupils in grades one to seven should not be given access to generative AI, while students in eight to 10 should be introduced to it gradually.

Australia has taken another route: a national framework for responsible and ethical use of generative AI in schools, rather than a blanket prohibition. The European Union, meanwhile, has sought to regulate high-risk uses of AI. Under the EU AI Act, certain systems used in education — including those involved in evaluating learning outcomes or determining access to education — can fall into the high-risk category. The legislation does not amount to a general ban on generative AI in schools.

Poland is going further in the opposite direction, investing almost 1.9 billion zloty to equip 12,000 schools with AI laboratory sets as part of its broader digital education push.

And where does India stand? India is closer to the integration camp. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 identifies artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies as important to India’s changing educational and employment landscape, and calls for contemporary subjects such as AI to be introduced at appropriate stages, alongside greater emphasis on computational thinking.

The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) introduced Artificial Intelligence as an optional sixth subject in Class IX from the 2019-20 academic session. More recently, for 2026-27, CBSE launched a dedicated Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence curriculum for Classes III to VIII, with AI and allied-subject curricula for Classes IX to XII also finalised. The curriculum emphasises logical reasoning, pattern recognition, algorithm design, data literacy and responsible and ethical AI use.

Kennedy pointed to findings from Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, who confirmed Friday that the six-week-old child died from measles last month.

"The Lancaster County Coroner has now publicly stated that measles caused only the second infant's death," Kennedy wrote on social media.

The child was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare genetic disorder that can lead to viral infections and typically results in death within months of birth.

In a post on social media, Kennedy fired back at Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) after he accused Kennedy of directing the Centers for Disease and Prevention (CDC) to not acknowledge the deaths in federal data.

"The facts emerging now demonstrate why CDC waited for the evidence rather than allowing political grandstanding to dictate its reporting," Kennedy wrote in a response Friday. "Governor Shapiro, by contrast, politicized these two tragic deaths before the underlying causes had been established."

Pennsylvania health officials announced last week that two unvaccinated individuals had died in connection to the state's measles outbreak, which has sickened 577 people and hospitalized 98.

The coroner drew a distinction between the two cases, which both involved infants.

In one case, a forensic pathologist determined the infant had died from a ruptured spleen and did not conclude that measles caused the death. In the second case, Diamantoni said a review of the 6-week-old infant's medical records established that measles was the cause of death.

title: Exclusive-Kennedy asked to remove Pennsylvania measles death from CDC tally, sources say
description: U.S. Health Secretary Robert F.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 3 (Reuters) - U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked his new CDC director to remove a reference to two Pennsylvania deaths from the agency's online measles tally after he questioned whether the disease contributed to the fatalities, three sources familiar with the situation said.

Kennedy's request came after CDC staffers had already ‌accepted the state's characterization of the deaths as linked to measles, a Pennsylvania official said.

Despite that, Erica Schwartz, the recently appointed director of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, ‌agreed with Kennedy's directive and implemented it without objection, said the three sources familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The move followed a heated exchange on social media between Kennedy, a long-time anti-vaccine activist appointed by President Donald Trump, and Pennsylvania ​Governor Josh Shapiro, a Democrat. The two officials accused each other of politicizing the outbreak in Pennsylvania, the latest state to grapple with a resurgence of measles since the Trump administration took office.

Data from the CDC and from individual states shows that vaccine rates have been declining, with many medical organizations citing rising vaccine hesitancy as a major cause. In Pennsylvania alone, the state health department has reported 540 measles cases this year.

Georges Benjamin, chief executive of the American Public Health Association and formerly Maryland's secretary of health, said it is "unheard of" for the CDC to publicly raise doubts about the conclusions of state and local health departments, even if the agency seeks more information.

"The secretary ‌had no business interfering in the normal process," Benjamin said. "He has an ⁠anti-vaccine agenda and he's using this to play out his anti-vaccine agenda."

Grace Davis Jamison, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services which oversees CDC, said the public health agency "requested details necessary to determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths." She cited conflicting reports between county and state health officials over what ⁠had transpired. Jamison did not comment on Kennedy's or Schwartz's role in excluding the deaths. Schwartz did not respond to a request for comment.

Kennedy has for years promoted the idea that vaccines are more dangerous than the diseases they prevent, despite decades of scientific evidence that they save lives. The combined measles, mumps and rubella shot routinely given to U.S. children has been shown to provide 97% protection against infection.

As health secretary, Kennedy has sought to minimize the impact ​of ​rising U.S. measles cases, now at their highest level in more than three decades. He has repeatedly cast doubt on whether ​the virus was directly related to the several deaths reported so far.

The Pennsylvania health department notified the CDC of two measles-associated deaths on the morning of August 25 and then made the news public on its website, according to the Pennsylvania official, who is close to Shapiro.

Pennsylvania did not share information about the circumstances of the deaths other than that the two individuals were unvaccinated. The CDC did not express concern over the information it had received and "signified its ongoing support for the (state health) department's efforts," the official said.

Kennedy called Shapiro by phone and offered federal support to assist with the state's measles outbreak, the governor said at a press conference later that day. Shapiro said he thanked Kennedy and said the state had implemented an aggressive response, including existing support from CDC and HHS staff, but that he would let the secretary know if they needed more help.

Shapiro also said he told Kennedy that ‌the health secretary's past statements encouraged conspiracy theories and misinformation about the safety of vaccines, "having a negative impact on communities ​across America."

Kennedy fired back on X the following day, August 26, accusing Shapiro of refusing to share information with the CDC ​and questioning whether the deaths were "altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers."

That same day, ​the Pennsylvania health department discussed some details of the two cases with the CDC, the official close to Shapiro said. The CDC asked for health records that contained ‌personally identifiable information about the deceased, which the state is legally barred from ​sharing, the Pennsylvania official said. The state offered to provide ​more de-identified information to CDC, but the federal agency has not signed off on the required paperwork, the official added.

A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania health department said the state has "provided all required epidemiological data to the CDC."

On Friday, the CDC delayed its regular weekly update to its measles data website. When it updated the page on Sunday, it did not include the Pennsylvania fatalities but ​added an asterisk to its table on deaths with the following note: "At ‌this time, available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the (Pennsylvania) deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles."

The CDC has not ​indicated what information it will use to determine whether the Pennsylvania deaths were caused by measles, since it is not working with the state health department in its investigation.

title: 10 Apple Health Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
description: You don't need an Apple Watch to get great health insights from Apple.
fullText:
Even if you’ve never opened the Apple Health app, if you have an iPhone, you’ve probably used apps that send information to its on-phone database. Apple Health is a powerful tool for controlling who gets access to your health data, logging data in different ways, and even taking at-home screening tests for certain health issues. If you have an Apple Watch, that’s great, but you don’t need one (or any wearable!) to take advantage of most of these 10 hacks to get more out of the Apple Health app.

Before we get into the other hacks, I’d like to discuss just how private your Apple Health data is (or isn’t). Apple provides its Health privacy policy here, and it says that your data lives on your own device and is encrypted when your phone is locked. There are some exceptions, though, which you can turn on or off. Here are the main things you may want to check on:

Individual apps can ask for permission to read data from Apple Health. (They also need your permission to write data to it.) You can control per-app permissions in Settings. Or, for a specific data point (like “walking and running distance”), go to that area of Apple Health and tap Data Sources and Access.

You can back up your health data via iCloud, which means it will live on Apple’s servers so you can access it from any of your devices. It is encrypted so Apple cannot read it. Manage this from your iCloud settings (in Settings, under your name).

You can share health data with your doctor or with people you know, like family members. To manage who has access, go to the Health app and tap the Sharing tab.

During workouts, some data from your workout may appear in a Live Activity widget on your lock screen. To hide this data while your phone is locked, go to the Settings app, tap Face ID & Passcode, and then under Allow Access When Locked, toggle Workout Health Data.

Your Medical ID may be available when your device is locked. (This is how bystanders and first responders can access your emergency contact or other information you’d like to remain available in emergencies.) To control access to this, go to the Health app, find Medical ID, and toggle Show When Locked.

The Health app includes a built-in medication tracker with a number of hidden features. Browse or search for Medications, and set up tracking by adding a medication, or anything else. You can type in the name, or use your camera to scan the bottle’s label. (This also works for over-the-counter meds and supplements, like if you want to be sure to take a vitamin every day.) I like that you can customize a pill-shaped icon to match a pill’s appearance.

Next, you can set up reminders. From this screen, you can tell the app when you plan to take your medication (if it’s one you take regularly, rather than as needed). The Health app will notify you at that time. To make the most of this feature, I recommend setting up follow-up reminders, which you’ll find on a different screen as well—more about that below.

After you set up your medications, scroll to the bottom of the medications screen and tap Pin to Summary. Now you just have to open the Health app and tap Medications to see a list of what you need to take today. You can also log via Siri, including batched logging like “Siri, log that I took my 10 a.m. meds” so you don’t have to list each one.

At the bottom of the Medications screen, you can tap Options and turn on Follow Up Reminders, which will give you an extra notification 30 minutes after the first one if you haven’t logged a dose. I use this feature all the time myself: I get the first reminder while I’m in the middle of doing something, eventually take the pill, then the follow-up reminds me to log it. If I got distracted along the way, I have a second chance to not miss a dose.

Another handy feature here is the Export PDF button at the bottom of the page, which will print out a list of all your current medications so you can bring it to your medical appointments or anywhere else you need to.

If you’re not familiar with the Health app, you might not think there’s much there—just a few things on the home screen. You can change that, but it takes a few steps. You see, rather than being a minimalist app, there’s so much available in Health that Apple figures it’s not worth giving you a big list to start off. Tap the magnifying glass icon in the lower right corner, and you’ll see a whole list of categories. You can search from this screen, or browse the categories.

Definitely take a minute to browse through these and see what features you might actually use. If you track what you eat in an Apple Health-connected app, you’ll be able to see all the individual components here: how much protein you’ve gotten today, for instance. Anything that a wearable can track is on here, including things you probably didn’t realize. I have a grade for my walking steadiness, for example.

Once you’ve figured out which of these hundreds of data points are actually useful, put the ones you care about on the main app screen (called Summary). Find a relevant card by searching or browsing, scroll to the bottom, and tap Pin to Summary. This way you can see exactly what you want when you open the app: say, your steps, protein intake, and the day’s medications. (Plus a few things you may want to add after you learn about them below...)

A lot of us are nervous about logging reproductive health data anywhere that may not be private. I’ve written that Euki may be the best standalone app for privacy, but you don’t need to use an app at all: Tracking directly in Apple Health means that your data is encrypted and lives on your phone, subject to the privacy features discussed above.

To use the built-in tracker, go to the magnifying glass and tap (or search for) Cycle Tracking. The cycle tracker on this screen (which you can pin to your summary) allows you to log menstrual bleeding, as well as “factors” like contraceptive use, pregnancy, and more.

Under the Options at the bottom of this screen, you can turn on period predictions, fertile window estimates, and more. I recommend enabling the Symptoms log if you’d like to keep track of things like cramps and nausea. You can also decide if you want Apple Health to use your temperature and heart rate data from a wearable for better cycle detection.

Another surprising use for manual logging in the Health app is under Mental Wellbeing. This is a really useful screen, since it collects things known to affect mental health, like your sleep, exercise minutes, time in daylight, and more. From here, you can also set up emotion and mood logging. The app explains that it considers emotions to be how you feel right now, and moods are how you’ve felt overall that day.

You can turn on reminders to log your moods. The default is to log twice per day: once around midday, and once at the end of the day. Scroll to the bottom of the Mental Wellbeing screen to set up logging.  Once you’ve set it up, it will appear as State of Mind; you may want to pin this to your summary. You can even view graphs of your state of mind over time, and see what other factors they associate with. A really useful view is to tap Show in Charts and then highlight Life Factors so you can see if your moods seem to track your exercise minutes or your hours of sleep.

The Health app also includes a built-in hearing test, but it requires AirPods Pro 3 (or AirPods Pro 2). To find the hearing test, look up Hearing in the Health app, then Get More From Health, and then Take Hearing Test. This will only be available if you have the right type of headphones connected. Follow the prompts to take the test. Apple has more information on this test here. If your results seem concerning, you can export a PDF of your results to discuss with a professional.

Accessing your medical records through patient portals can be annoying. Instead, you can import your digital medical records directly into the Health app, giving you quick access to your medical history as needed. Apple offers a list of the healthcare systems whose data it can access.

It’s worth looking over the privacy policies for this feature as well, but the good news is that the data follows an encrypted connection between your phone and the healthcare organization, without ever giving Apple (the company) access to it. I’d recommend turning off Improve Health Records, which sends an anonymized version of your data to Apple; health records are detailed information about your body—but feel free to leave it on if that’s your preference. You can back up your health data over iCloud, as discussed above.

As with menstrual cycle tracking, it can be useful to any health data directly in the app. You can actually do this with just about any data point: just view that type of data, and then tap the plus sign in the upper right corner. Think you took about 1,000 steps when you had your watch off? Just tap the plus on the Steps screen and add them.

A handy place to use this feature is for blood pressure tracking. Some wearables estimate your blood pressure, like Whoop and the Samsung Galaxy Watch. But you don’t need one of those to log your numbers: just take note of your blood pressure at the doctor’s office, or when you use a wrist cuff or one of those machines they sometimes have at pharmacies. Open Blood Pressure and tap the plus, then put in the new reading. You’ll be able to view your history of blood pressure readings, and even see charts of how it has changed over time.

Some medications affect your heart rate, most notably beta blockers and calcium channel blockers. If you’re taking one of those, your heart rate won’t match Apple’s general-purpose formulas for gauging your cardio fitness (a VO2max estimate) from your heart rate. You’ll appear to have a higher cardio fitness than you actually have.

To let Apple account for this, go to your profile picture, tap Health Details, tap Edit at the top of the page, and scroll down to Medications That Affect Heart Rate. You can select calcium channel blockers or beta blockers, or both; these are the only categories of medication that Apple can account for.

There’s a Medical ID feature that can be accessed from your lock screen even without unlocking your phone. It’s a great place to put your emergency contact information, but to make the most use of it, you need the people in your life to know how to access the information and what’s in there.

I first learned about the Medical ID when I was teaching a class. A student came up to tell me about a medical condition, and showed me how to access her Medical ID (it’s right at the bottom of the lock screen). Most importantly, she made sure I knew what information I’d be able to find there, so I knew when and whether to reach for it in an emergency.

I’d advise that you do the same if you want to be prepared. Besides allergies and contact information, the Medical ID field can include information on whether you’re pregnant, what medications you take, any medical conditions you’d like to disclose, and your height, weight, and blood type. There’s also an area at the bottom for notes, where you can add any information you feel is critical.

Also consider whether you want to turn on Share During Emergency Call, which allows this information to be shared with emergency services. You can also control whether or not your Medical ID appears on your lock screen using a separate toggle.

title: Breakaway Holiday Classic will feature five high school games, three state finalists
description: The high school basketball Breakaway Holiday Classic will be five-game event at Noblesville's Riverview Health Arena
fullText:
The second annual Breakaway Holiday Classic presented by Citizens State Bank will feature five high school basketball games, including three state finalists from last season.

Sheridan is coming off a 19-5 season and will return all-state senior Trey Page, who averaged 19.3 points per game last season and shot 39% from the 3-point line. Seniors Desh Donathan and John Crowder also return. Sheridan is a Class 2A program. Liberty Christian went 19-8 last season, falling in a 2-point game in the semistate to eventual Class 1A state champion Barr-Reeve. The Lions should again be one of the top teams in 1A with Kendrick Martin (17.8 ppg, 4.5 rebounds) and others returning.

Both teams played in the state finals last season. Barr-Reeve went 28-1 and won the Class 1A state title, while Westview came up just short against Parke Heritage in the 2A game, falling 57-56. Barr-Reeve returns all five starters from last year's team, including senior Kierson Lengacher (14.0 ppg) and juniors Jaylon Graber (10.8 ppg, 4.0 rebounds) and Braxton Neidigh (9.9 ppg). Westview brings back senior standout Austin Schlabach (19.5 ppg, 5.7 assists), a Huntington commit.

"We are excited for our matchup against a historic program like Barr-Reeve. It should be a great battle between two really good programs," Westview coach Chandler Prible said.

Lawrence North is coming off four consecutive seasons of at least 18 wins. This team will be a little on the young side with juniors Chandon Gilbert (10.2 ppg) and Davis Baker (6.0 ppg, 40.4% 3-pointers) the top returning scorers. Talked freshman Levin Robinson will also be a key player for Lawrence North. Fort Wayne Snider will return four starters from a 20-8 squad, including Trell Hogue (11.5 ppg), Ketron Paschall (8.8 ppg, 6.5 rebounds) and Chance DeRossett (8.3 ppg, 3.4 rebounds).

"We are so excited to be able to play a great opponent in a professional arena. These are the type of games that help prepare a team for the tournament and we are excited to test ourselves with a high-level opponent," Snider coach Joshua Riikonen said.

Guerin is coming off a 21-6 season and returns four starters for a squad that should be among the best in Class 3A. Jake Grissom (20.5 ppg, 4.5 rebounds), a Junior All-Star last season, will lead the Golden Eagles, along with seniors Carter Murans (12.4 ppg, 4.6 rebounds) and Hayden Rogers (8.1 ppg, 7.0 assists). "We are excited to be included in an event that features some of the best teams in Indiana and thankful for the opportunity to play in one of the premier venues in Hamilton County," Guerin coach Sam Gardner said. "We have great respect for Coach Jones and a New Albany team that will be a 4A title contender this year."

The Bulldogs were 25-2 last season. Hamilton Southeastern is coming off a 15-10 season last year and brings back junior Varschon Clark (13.3 ppg, 4.6 rebounds) and sophomore K.J. Buckley (3.3 ppg), among others.

"Crown Point is thrilled and honored to be playing in the 2027 Breakaway Holiday Classic. The opportunity to play a great program like Hamilton Southeastern in a venue like Riverview Health Arena are just the type of opportunities we seek out for our players," said Crown Point coach Clint Swan. "It promises to be a great day of basketball and a memorable experience for all."

title: Asia’s aging population will redefine retirement, care—and independence
description: Adults in Asia are increasingly prioritizing autonomy, health, and financial security over maximizing the inheritance they leave behind.
fullText:
Over the next decade, Asian families will transfer an estimated $10 trillion—nearly twice the size of Germany's GDP—to the next generation. Yet there's a nuanced story emerging behind that headline figure. As people live longer, they're rethinking how preserve their own independence while still passing enough wealth to their children.

What percentage of assets are Asians reserving for themselves?

Why are traditional family care models under pressure?

How is longer life expectancy changing wealth transfer patterns?

What financial solutions could support independent aging strategies?

Asia is the fastest-aging region in the world. Fifteen percent of its population is over the age of 60; that share is projected to rise to 26% by 2050, according to the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific. Some of the world's longest-living populations are also in Asia, led by Hong Kong, where life expectancy is 85.5 years. In mainland China, life expectancy rose from around 52 in 1963 to 78 today.

This transformation isn't just a demographic story. Greater longevity is reshaping how people think about wealth, care, and responsibility within the family.

For generations, many in Asia assumed that wealth would be passed to children, through the funding of education and home ownership, or leaving an eventual inheritance—with children later caring for their parents in old age. But today's families are planning things differently. Our data shows that adults in Asia are increasingly prioritizing autonomy, health, and financial security over maximizing the inheritance they leave behind.

The next chapter of Asia's wealth transfer won't be defined only by the money parents leave behind. It will also be measured by something potentially more valuable: the freedom to support their own longer, more independent lives—and, in turn, relieve their children of the financial and emotional burdens of caregiving.

Manulife's Asia Care Survey 2026 of 9,000 adults across nine Asia markets, shows how far this shift towards independence has progressed. Men in Asia anticipate funding 14 years of their own care in later life, and women 15 years, at a time when fewer older people than ever are living with their adult children.

The survey's respondents overwhelmingly value independence and financial freedom over passing down tangible assets to their family. Regionwide, 83% said securing that freedom was more important than leaving their heirs the maximum amount of wealth.

Respondents plan to earmark an average of 68% of their money and assets to fund their own costs, including health care, as they age, leaving the rest to their children. This ratio varied across markets, with those in Taiwan expecting to spend the most on their own health and care at 78%, and those in the Philippines and Indonesia planning to spend the least, both at 60%.

title: Baby goats with rabies at North Carolina mobile petting zoo prompt calls across multiple counties to contact health officials
description: Several baby goats at a mobile petting zoo in North Carolina were infected with rabies, and authorities are asking anyone who had contact with the animals to reach out to health officials about potent...
fullText:
Multiple baby goats at a mobile petting zoo in North Carolina were infected with rabies, and authorities are asking anyone who had contact with the animals to reach out to health officials about potential exposure to the rare but deadly virus.

Residents in western North Carolina may have been exposed to the infected goats from Farm Adventures at the mobile petting zoo's location in Harmony or at off-site events between July 28 and August 27, local officials said in a statement. The state has not reported human cases of the virus since 2011.

Exposure may have happened at 10 locations, including an assisted living facility and back-to-school bash, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services said. Those affected are urged to contact their local health department to determine whether they need medication to prevent infection.

The goats were most likely exposed to rabies by a skunk that had entered their pen in late July, according to the state health department, which was first notified of the rabies exposure on Thursday.

Lab testing found the virus in three of the baby goats, and a fourth is also assumed to have been infected, state officials said.

Farm Adventures is based in Iredell County and books events in surrounding communities, and officials say the owner has been cooperating with the investigation.

"There is not a broad risk to the public — only those who attended events at the mobile petting zoo and were in close contact with the goats are at risk," officials said.

"Residents should not wait for symptoms before calling," Mecklenburg County Health Director Kimberly Scott said.

Scott told CNN a coordinated statewide investigation is still seeking "specifics on total reach across counties and total number of people impacted." Communicable disease teams across multiple counties are alerting the public and working with the petting zoo to contact event organizers.

She said healthcare systems appear to have enough postexposure prophylaxis (PEP), the typical rabies treatment, available, and officials are "positioned to acquire access to more as needed as we learn more information."

"What's important is that we don't wait for the onset of symptoms when it is more difficult to treat and often most fatal," Scott said.

Farm Adventures said its "4 precious baby goats" were euthanized and its staff is "closely monitoring our remaining animals under the guidelines provided by health officials." The goats had been kept in a separate pen because they were too young for vaccinations, the petting zoo said.

"I care about my community, and I care about my customers," Misty Love, the owner of Farm Adventures, told CNN on Saturday. "If my customers that saw my animals have questions, I'm going to be there for them."

Love said a wild skunk was found in the goat enclosure on July 29, and the animal was shot and burned. The goats did not appear to have been bitten and showed no signs of rabies, according to Love. But one goat died on August 19. The next day, she said, another goat became ill and was euthanized.

A necropsy on one of the animals revealed the infection.

"RIP Molly, Maggie, cow and Uno," the zoo's post said.

Since confirming the virus, state officials say they have been working with the farm and local health departments to find out when and where residents were exposed.

Animals from the petting zoo were at the Masonic Picnic in Mocksville on August 15, according to a Facebook post from Davie County Health and Human Services. Additionally, Catawba and Burke counties said the petting zoo was at a private event near Hickory on August 9. Another event at Breeden Amphitheater in Lexington on August 1 included the petting zoo, according to the Davidson County Health Department.

Other potential exposure sites included private events in Mecklenburg, Watauga, Durham and Iredell counties, according to the state health department.

State health officials said they are working with event organizers to notify attendees who may have had contact with the infected goats.

No other animals on the farm pose a risk of rabies exposure to people, the department said.

Though human cases of rabies in the United States are rare, the disease can be deadly if people don't receive treatment before symptoms begin. Fewer than 10 deaths are reported each year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Rabies is caused by a virus that is spread mainly through the saliva of infected animals. This virus is typically transmitted through an animal bite, though scratches or direct contact with mucosa can also spread the virus.

The virus primarily affects the central nervous system, with inflammation of the brain and spinal cord. The incubation period, the time between exposure to the virus and symptom onset, can last weeks to months. Once a person starts showing symptoms of rabies, the disease is nearly always fatal.

During incubation, there are typically no symptoms. Weeks to months after exposure, an infected person may experience flu-like symptoms that can include fever, headache and overall body aches. Discomfort, such as a prickling sensation, at the site of the bite is also possible.

Rabies is preventable but requires vaccination or immediate medical attention after exposure, according to the CDC. Postexposure prophylaxis is highly effective if received soon after exposure.

Rabies transmission from livestock holds a lower risk than bites from wild animals, but people can still be exposed to the virus through saliva from an infected animal, the North Carolina health department said.

"Because baby goats are frequently bottle-fed, handled closely, or cuddled, public health officials are working proactively to ensure anyone who had direct contact with the affected animals is evaluated," the department said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Jamie Gumbrecht and Dianne Gallagher contributed to this report.

It was truly a dominating night for the Indiana Fever, as they picked up an 111-91 win over the Connecticut Sun on Friday.

The story of the game was the combination of Fever guards Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell, each scoring 34 points in the win. Clark had a double-double as well with 12 assists, 5 rebounds, and 3 steals. She made history as the first WNBA player to ever have consecutive games with 30+ points and 10+ assists double-doubles.

One concern about Clark was her back injury, which has lingered for the last two months. With the World Cup around the corner and Clark about to play for Team USA, many wonder how her health is.

Clark had a chance to speak with the media after the Fever beat the Sun. She was asked about her health, and it was the kind of update that Fever fans needed to hear.

"I feel probably the best I've ever felt in my career," Clark said. "It was battle for like the first 20 games for me to really find my confidence again, mostly in my body. Now, I feel like I'm just playing. I'm not thinking."

#Fever star Caitlin Clark on her back/overall health:

“I feel probably the best I’ve ever felt in my career …”

“It was battle for like the first 20 games for me to really find my confidence again, mostly in my body. Now, I feel like I’m just playing. I’m not thinking.” pic.twitter.com/i3c0jC15GV

— James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) August 29, 2026

In 36 games this season, Clark is averaging 22.5 points, 8.4 assists, 3.9 rebounds, and 1 steal per contest. She leads the WNBA in assists per game and is third in scoring.

The Fever enter the World Cup break with a 26-14 overall record and sit in fourth in the standings. They are 2.5 games behind the Golden State Valkyries for second in the playoff hunt.

Clark is about to take off to play in the World Cup for Team USA. The hope is that she can stay healthy with fewer minutes. Team USA will play as many of its players as possible. Clark could be looking at 15 to 20 minutes per game at most.

As for the rest of the Fever, they will use this time to rest and prepare for the last four games of the regular season. They won't be back in action until September 18 when they face the Toronto Tempo.
